title: Heart, blood and breath: the two circles inside you

summary.text: This unit is about your heart, your blood and your breathing. Your heart is a muscle, about the size of your fist. It squeezes about a hundred thousand times a day, and pushes blood round your body in a loop. Your lungs pull air in and push it out. In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen, a gas in the air that every part of you needs. Blood carries that oxygen, and food, to every tiny part of you, and carries waste away. You can feel all of this working: your pulse in your wrist, your chest rising and falling, and both speeding up when you run. Scientists know a lot about this pump and these air bags. But they still wonder why a human heart can hardly repair itself, and how our heartbeat and our feelings talk to each other.
summary.art: A child standing with one hand on the chest and one on the tummy, a see-through view showing a red heart, two pink lungs and red and blue loops of blood vessels spreading out to the hands and feet.

intro.hook: Sit very still. Put your hand flat on the middle of your chest, a little to the left. Wait, and do not talk. Can you feel something knocking? It has been knocking since before you were born. It has never once stopped. What is it doing?
intro.text: About 400 years ago, an English doctor called William Harvey did a sum. He guessed how much blood a heart pushes out with each beat. Then he counted the beats. In one hour, the heart pushed out more blood than the weight of a whole person. Where could all that blood come from? Where could it go? Harvey's answer changed medicine for ever. The same blood must go round and round, again and again. In this unit you will feel that circle, count it and hear it.
intro.art: A small child with eyes closed and a hand flat on the chest, and around the hand, faint ripple lines like a drum being struck.

outcomes: I can say that the heart is a muscle that pumps blood, and that blood goes round the body in a loop and comes back.
I can find my pulse, count it fairly, and show how exercise changes it in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain how we breathe: a muscle under the lungs pulls down, and air flows in. I can say that we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide.
I can say what blood is made of and what it carries: oxygen and food to every part of the body, and waste away.
I can explain why my heart and breathing speed up when I run or feel scared, and how slow breathing can calm my heart. I can name ways to keep my heart and lungs healthy.
I can tell how people found out about the heart and blood, from Galen to Ibn al-Nafis, William Harvey and Helen Taussig, and why their ideas changed.
I can explain that every part of me uses oxygen to get energy from food, that I share air with plants and people, and what scientists still do not know about hearts and breath.

terms.meaning: A muscle in the middle of your chest, tipped a little to the left. It squeezes again and again to push blood round your body.
terms.example: Your heart is about the size of your own fist. It beats about 100,000 times a day.
terms.art: A fist next to a heart shape of the same size, inside an outline of a child's chest.

terms.meaning: The red liquid that flows through tubes all over your body. It carries oxygen, food and warmth to every part of you, and carries waste away.
terms.example: When you scrape your knee, the red drops are blood.
terms.art: A drop of blood under a magnifying glass, showing it is full of tiny round red discs.

terms.meaning: A tube that blood flows through. Some are as thick as your thumb. Some are thinner than a hair.
terms.example: The blue-green lines you can see on the inside of your wrist are blood vessels.
terms.art: The inside of a wrist with thin blue-green lines under the skin.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart, out to the body. Its walls are thick and stretchy, because the heart pushes hard.
terms.example: The pulse you feel in your wrist is an artery stretching with each heartbeat.
terms.art: A thick red tube bulging a little as a pulse passes along it, an arrow pointing away from a heart.

terms.meaning: A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart.
terms.example: The lines you see on the back of your hand are veins.
terms.art: A thinner tube with an arrow pointing back towards a heart.

terms.meaning: The tiniest blood vessel, thinner than a hair. Capillaries reach every part of you. Here oxygen and food leave the blood and go into the body.
terms.example: Capillaries are why every tiny cut, anywhere on your skin, bleeds a little.
terms.art: A net of very fine red threads wrapped around a cluster of round cells.

terms.meaning: The beat you can feel where an artery is close to the skin. Each beat is one squeeze of your heart.
terms.example: Press two fingers gently on the thumb side of your wrist. The little taps are your pulse.
terms.art: Two fingers resting on the thumb side of a child's wrist, with tiny tap marks.

terms.meaning: One squeeze of the heart, and then a rest. Through a stethoscope it sounds like 'lub-dub'.
terms.example: A child sitting still has about 70 to 110 heartbeats in one minute.
terms.art: A heart with two small sound bubbles saying lub and dub.

terms.meaning: A little flap door inside the heart and veins. It lets blood go one way and snaps shut to stop it flowing back.
terms.example: The 'lub-dub' sound is the heart's valves snapping shut.
terms.art: A flap door swinging open one way, with a red arrow going through, and closed when the arrow tries to go back.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy bags in your chest. Air goes in and out of them when you breathe.
terms.example: When you take a deep breath, your chest gets bigger because your lungs are filling up.
terms.art: Two pink spongy lungs inside a rib cage, with a windpipe at the top like the trunk of a tree.

terms.meaning: The tube that carries air from your nose and mouth down to your lungs. It has stiff rings, so it never squashes flat.
terms.example: Touch the front of your neck gently. The bumpy rings you feel are your windpipe.
terms.art: A side view of a neck with a ringed tube going down to the lungs.

terms.meaning: Millions of tiny bubbles at the ends of the tubes inside your lungs. Scientists call them alveoli. Oxygen passes from the air in them into the blood.
terms.example: If you could spread all the air sacs of a grown-up flat, they would cover nearly a badminton court.
terms.art: A bunch of tiny grapes made of bubbles, each wrapped in a net of red capillaries.

terms.meaning: A big dome-shaped muscle under your lungs. When it pulls down, air flows into your lungs.
terms.example: Put your hand on your tummy and breathe in deeply. Your tummy pushes out because your diaphragm moves down.
terms.art: A dome-shaped muscle sitting under two lungs, with an arrow pulling it flat.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air, with no colour and no smell. Every part of your body needs it to get energy from food.
terms.example: Plants and tiny sea creatures called algae put oxygen into the air.
terms.art: A leaf giving off small bubbles marked O, which drift towards a child's nose.

terms.meaning: A gas that your body makes as waste when it uses food for energy. You breathe it out. Plants take it in.
terms.example: When you breathe out onto a cold steel plate, some of what leaves you is carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A child breathing out small grey bubbles which drift towards a tulsi plant.

terms.meaning: Tiny round discs in blood that carry oxygen. They are what make blood red. A drop of blood holds millions of them.
terms.example: Red blood cells contain iron. That is one reason we need iron-rich food like spinach, jaggery and dal.
terms.art: Many red discs, dented in the middle like a doughnut that was pressed by a thumb.

terms.meaning: The way blood goes round and round your body in a loop, pushed by the heart, and comes back to the heart.
terms.example: A drop of blood leaving your heart is back again in about one minute.
terms.art: A big loop like a ring road, with a heart as the pump at one side and red arrows going round.

terms.meaning: What every tiny part of your body does with oxygen. It uses oxygen to break up food and get energy out. Carbon dioxide is left over.
terms.example: When you run, your leg muscles do a lot of respiration. So you breathe faster to get more oxygen.
terms.art: A tiny cell, like a little room, taking in a sugar shape and an oxygen bubble, and giving out a spark of energy and a carbon dioxide bubble.

terms.meaning: A tool doctors use to listen to the heart and lungs. It carries the tiny sounds through a tube to their ears.
terms.example: The first stethoscope, made in 1816, was a rolled-up tube of paper.
terms.art: A doctor's stethoscope next to a rolled-up paper tube.

terms.meaning: The pale yellow watery part of blood. The blood cells float in it. It carries food, water and salts.
terms.example: If blood is left to stand in a tube, the red cells sink and the yellow plasma stays on top.
terms.art: A test tube with a dark red layer at the bottom and a straw-coloured layer on top.

explanations.definition: The heart is a hollow muscle that squeezes and relaxes again and again. Each squeeze pushes blood out into tubes that go all over the body.
explanations.description: A pump is anything that pushes a liquid along. A hand pump at a village well is a pump. So is a squeezy bottle. Your heart is a pump made of muscle. It is hollow inside, like a small bag with thick walls. When the walls squeeze, blood is pushed out. When the walls relax, the heart fills up with blood again. Then it squeezes again. It never needs you to remember. It has been doing this since before you were born, and it rests only for a moment between beats.
examples: Squeeze a water-filled balloon or a squeezy bottle. Water shoots out. That is a pump.
A hand pump on a well pushes water up a pipe each time you press the handle.
Your heart is about the size of your fist. Make a fist and squeeze it tight, then open it. That is roughly what your heart does, about once every second.
explanations.art: A hollow heart shown half-open like a cut fruit, thick muscle walls squeezing, with red arrows of blood shooting out of the top.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the heart: it is a muscle pump.

explanations.concept: Blood goes round in two circles
explanations.definition: Circulation is the way blood travels from the heart, round the body, and back to the heart, again and again. In people it goes round two loops, one through the lungs and one through the rest of the body.
explanations.description: Your heart has four rooms inside, two on the right and two on the left. The right side pushes blood a short way, to the lungs. There the blood picks up oxygen and becomes bright red. Then it comes back to the left side of the heart. The left side pushes it out to the whole body: your brain, your toes, your fingertips. There the oxygen is used up. The blood, now darker red, comes back to the right side of the heart. Then it goes to the lungs again. So it is like a figure of eight, with the heart in the middle. A drop of blood goes all the way round in about one minute while you sit still.
examples: The left side of the heart has a thicker wall than the right. It must push blood all the way to your toes. The right side only pushes it next door, to the lungs.
Think of a ring road round a city with a petrol pump in the middle. The blood is the traffic. It keeps coming back to the pump.
If you laid all the blood vessels of a grown-up end to end, scientists guess they might stretch around 100,000 kilometres. That is more than twice round the Earth. Nobody has measured this exactly.
explanations.art: A figure-of-eight loop: a heart in the middle, the top loop going to two pink lungs and turning bright red, the bottom loop going to a child's body and turning darker red.
explanations.context: This card explains circulation: how blood goes out from the heart and always comes back, round two loops.

explanations.concept: What blood is, and what it carries
explanations.definition: Blood is a liquid made of watery plasma with billions of tiny cells floating in it. It carries oxygen, food, water and warmth to every part of the body, and carries waste away.
explanations.description: Blood looks like one red liquid. Under a microscope it is a crowd. Most of the crowd are red blood cells. They are tiny round discs that carry oxygen. They contain iron, and that iron is what grabs the oxygen. There are also white blood cells, which fight germs. You will meet them properly in the unit on how the body fights germs. There are tiny pieces called platelets, which stick together to plug a cut. All of these float in plasma, a pale yellow watery liquid. Plasma carries the food from your lunch, water and salts. An 8-year-old child has about 2 litres of blood, about the same as a big water bottle.
examples: When you get a cut, platelets clump together and make a scab.
Red blood cells only live about four months. Your bones make new ones all the time. A grown-up makes about 2 million new red cells every second.
The food you ate at lunch soaks into your blood from your gut. Blood then carries it to your muscles and brain.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drop of blood: many red discs, a few larger white blobs, tiny flat platelets, all floating in pale yellow liquid.
explanations.context: This card explains what blood is made of, and the jobs each part does.

explanations.concept: How we breathe in and out
explanations.definition: Breathing is moving air into the lungs and out again. A dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, the diaphragm, pulls down to make room, and air flows in. When it relaxes, air flows out.
explanations.description: Lungs have no muscles of their own. They cannot pull air in by themselves. So how does air get in? Under your lungs is the diaphragm, a muscle shaped like an upside-down bowl. When you breathe in, it pulls down and flattens. Your rib muscles lift your ribs out, too. Your chest gets bigger, so there is more room inside. The air outside presses in through your nose, down your windpipe and into the lungs, to fill that room. When you breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and goes back up. The space gets smaller, and air is squeezed out. So you do not really suck air in. You make room, and the air around you pushes in.
examples: Put a hand on your tummy and breathe in slowly. Your tummy pushes out. That is the diaphragm moving down and pushing your stomach out of the way.
A hiccup is your diaphragm jumping suddenly, by itself. The 'hic' is your voice box snapping shut.
When you blow up a balloon, the air comes from your lungs, squeezed out by your diaphragm and ribs.
explanations.art: Two side-by-side drawings of a chest: breathing in, the diaphragm flat and air arrows rushing in through the nose, and breathing out, the diaphragm domed and arrows going out.
explanations.context: This card explains how breathing works, using the muscle under the lungs called the diaphragm.

explanations.concept: The great swap in the lungs
explanations.definition: In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air. This happens in millions of tiny air sacs.
explanations.description: Your windpipe splits into two tubes, one for each lung. Each tube splits again and again, like the branches of a tree, into thousands of tiny tubes. At the very end of each tiny tube is a bunch of air bubbles called air sacs. A grown-up has hundreds of millions of them. Each air sac is wrapped in a net of capillaries, the tiniest blood vessels. The walls between the air and the blood are thinner than a soap bubble. So oxygen slips from the air into the blood. Carbon dioxide, the waste gas, slips the other way, out of the blood and into the air. Then you breathe it out. All this happens in less than a second, with every breath.
examples: The air you breathe in has about 21 parts oxygen in every 100. The air you breathe out still has about 16 parts. You only take a little each breath. That is why a rescuer's breath can still help someone who has stopped breathing.
The air you breathe out has about 100 times more carbon dioxide than the air you breathe in.
Spread flat, all the air sacs of a grown-up's lungs would cover nearly a badminton court. That huge surface is how so much oxygen gets in so fast.
explanations.art: A tree of tubes turning into bunches of tiny bubble-grapes, one bubble enlarged with red capillaries around it, blue dots of oxygen going in and grey dots of carbon dioxide coming out.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens inside the lungs: oxygen goes into the blood, and carbon dioxide comes out.

explanations.concept: Why every part of you needs oxygen
explanations.definition: Respiration is how the tiny living parts of your body, called cells, use oxygen to break up food and release its energy. Carbon dioxide and water are left over.
explanations.description: Your body is made of trillions of tiny living parts called cells. Each one is like a tiny busy room. Every cell needs energy to do its job. A muscle cell needs energy to pull. A brain cell needs energy to send messages. The energy is locked inside food, like the sugar from a banana. To unlock it, the cell needs oxygen. The cell joins food and oxygen together, and energy comes out. Carbon dioxide and water are left over. This is called respiration. It is a little like a fire, which also needs fuel and oxygen. But it is slow and gentle, and gives warmth, not flames. That is why you breathe. Breathing is the way oxygen reaches your cells, and the way carbon dioxide leaves.
examples: About 240 years ago, the French scientist Antoine Lavoisier showed that breathing is like a very slow burning. Animals take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide and heat, just like a candle does.
You are warm partly because of respiration. Trillions of cells releasing energy all day make heat.
Plants respire too, day and night. In sunlight they also make far more oxygen than they use.
explanations.art: A tiny cell drawn as a little kitchen: a banana-sugar shape and an oxygen bubble going in, a spark of energy and a warm glow and a grey carbon dioxide bubble coming out.
explanations.context: This card explains why we need oxygen at all: every cell uses it to get energy from food.

explanations.definition: Your pulse is the bump you feel in an artery each time the heart squeezes blood into it. The 'lub-dub' sound is the heart's valves snapping shut.
explanations.description: Each time your heart squeezes, a push of blood rushes into your arteries. Arteries are stretchy, a bit like a cycle tube. They bulge a little with each push, and then spring back. Where an artery runs close to the skin, you can feel that bulge with your fingers. That is your pulse. You can feel it on the thumb side of your wrist, at the side of your neck, and even on top of your foot. Inside the heart are flap doors called valves. They let blood go forward and stop it from going back. When they snap shut, they make a sound. The first snap is 'lub'. The second, a moment later, is 'dub'. Doctors listen to these sounds to check that the doors are closing well.
examples: Count your pulse for 30 seconds and double it. That gives your heartbeats in one minute.
A doctor presses a stethoscope on your chest and listens for 'lub-dub'. A swishing sound can mean a valve is leaking a little.
A garden hose jerks a little when someone squeezes the tap on and off. Your arteries jerk with each heartbeat in the same way.
explanations.art: Two fingers on a wrist with a magnified artery underneath bulging as a red push passes, beside a heart with two flap doors closing.
explanations.context: This card explains what your pulse is, and what makes the 'lub-dub' sound of a heartbeat.

explanations.concept: Why your heart and breath speed up when you run
explanations.definition: When muscles work hard they need more oxygen and food, and they make more carbon dioxide. So the heart beats faster and harder, and you breathe faster and deeper.
explanations.description: Sitting still, your muscles need only a little oxygen. When you run, your leg muscles are working very hard. They are burning food quickly, so they need much more oxygen. They also make a lot more carbon dioxide. Your brain notices the carbon dioxide building up in your blood. It sends messages to your heart to beat faster, and to your breathing muscles to work harder. After you stop, your heart and breath slowly come back down. A strong, fit heart pushes more blood with each beat. So it does not need to beat as fast. The same speeding up also happens when you feel scared or excited, even sitting still. Your body is getting ready to run, just in case.
examples: After a race, your heart can beat about twice as fast as when you rest.
The feeling that makes you want to breathe after holding your breath comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up, not from running out of oxygen.
Before a test or a big match, your heart may thump even though you are sitting down. Your body is getting ready to act.
explanations.art: A child running in a park, with a small heart icon beating fast, lungs puffing and arrows of oxygen rushing to the leg muscles.
explanations.context: This card explains why your heart and breathing get faster when you exercise, or feel scared.

explanations.concept: The heart starts its own beat
explanations.definition: The heart makes its own beat. A small patch of special cells in the heart sends out a tiny electric spark about once a second, and the whole heart squeezes.
explanations.description: You might think the brain tells the heart to beat each time. It does not. In the top of the heart's right side is a little patch of cells called the pacemaker. On its own, it makes a tiny electric spark, again and again. The spark spreads across the heart muscle, and the muscle squeezes. The brain can only tell the pacemaker to go faster or slower. Even a single heart muscle cell, kept alive in a dish in a laboratory, will twitch by itself in a beat. When a person gets a new heart from a donor, the nerves from the brain are not joined back. The new heart still beats, by its own spark.
examples: A doctor's heart machine, called an ECG, draws the heart's electric sparks as a wavy line.
Some people's pacemaker cells stop working well. They get a tiny battery-powered pacemaker that makes the spark for them.
Your heart started beating weeks before you were born, long before you had a brain that could think.
explanations.art: A heart with a small glowing spot at its top right sending a ripple of yellow electric light across the muscle, and beside it a wavy line on a screen.
explanations.context: This card explains what makes the heart beat: its own tiny electric spark, not a message from the brain each time.

explanations.concept: Why veins look blue when blood is red
explanations.definition: Blood is always red. Blood with lots of oxygen is bright red. Blood that has given its oxygen away is darker red. Veins only look blue because of the way skin and light work.
explanations.description: Look at the inside of your wrist. The veins look blue or green. Many people think the blood inside is blue until it touches air. That is not true. Blood is red all the time. Blood coming back to the heart has given away its oxygen, so it is a darker red, like beetroot juice. Light shining on your skin goes in a little way. Red light goes deep and is soaked up by the dark blood. Bluer light bounces back out more from that place. So the vein looks blue to your eye, even though the blood is dark red.
examples: When a nurse takes blood from a vein, it comes out dark red, not blue.
A pressed fingertip turns white, then pink again as blood flows back in.
Lobsters and octopuses really do have blue blood. They carry oxygen with copper instead of iron.
explanations.art: A wrist with blue-looking veins beside a small glass tube of dark red blood, and an arrow showing red light sinking into the skin and blue light bouncing out.
explanations.context: This card explains a common puzzle: why veins look blue when blood is always red.

explanations.concept: Breathing in, breathing out, and how they calm us
explanations.definition: Breathing happens by itself, but you can also take control of it. Slow breathing, especially a long breath out, gently slows the heart.
explanations.description: Most of the time you breathe without thinking, even when you sleep. A part of your brain near the back of your neck keeps it going. But you can also choose to breathe fast, slow or not at all for a short time. Breath is one of the few things in your body that runs by itself and also does what you tell it. Your heart and breath are linked. When you breathe in, your heart speeds up a tiny bit. When you breathe out, it slows a tiny bit. So a slow, long breath out gently calms the heart. This is why people in many countries use slow breathing to feel calm.
examples: Count your pulse. Then breathe in for 4 counts and out for 6 counts, ten times. Count again. Many people find their pulse has dropped a little.
Yoga teachers in India have taught slow, steady breathing for many centuries.
Babies and small children breathe faster than grown-ups. A sleeping baby may take 30 to 40 breaths a minute.
explanations.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, one hand on the belly, a soft wave line showing a long slow breath out and a calm heart beside it.
explanations.context: This card explains how breathing runs by itself, and how slow breathing can calm the heart.

explanations.concept: Why hearts beat at different speeds
explanations.description: A mouse's heart beats about 500 times a minute. An elephant's heart beats about 30 times. A human child's beats about 90. Small animals almost always have faster hearts. Scientists agree on that pattern. They argue about what it means, and especially about whether there is a 'budget' of heartbeats in a lifetime.
examples: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute while it flies.
In 2019, scientists stuck a sensor on a blue whale with suction cups. Deep under water, its heart beat only about 2 times a minute.
A newborn baby's heart beats about 120 to 160 times a minute. It slows down as the child grows.

perspectives.who: Many biologists who study animal size
perspectives.explanation: Small animals lose heat quickly, because they have a lot of skin for their size. So their cells must burn food fast to stay warm. Fast burning needs fast oxygen, so the heart beats fast. Big animals burn food slowly, so their hearts can be slow.
If you multiply heart rate by lifespan, many mammals end up with roughly a billion heartbeats in a life. A mouse spends them quickly, an elephant slowly. Maybe there is a kind of heartbeat budget.

The 'billion beats' pattern is rough, with many exceptions. Humans get two or three billion. Birds and bats live much longer than their heart speed suggests. A fit person's slower heart is healthier, but that does not mean each of us has a fixed number of beats. This idea is still argued about.

explanations.art: A row of animals from tiny to huge, a hummingbird, a mouse, a child, an elephant, a blue whale, each with a heart icon and a number of beats.
explanations.context: This card is about why different animals have different heart speeds, and an idea scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Is the heart where feelings live?
explanations.description: We say 'heartbroken', 'kind-hearted' and 'learn by heart'. For thousands of years, people thought the heart was where thinking and feeling happened. Today scientists agree that the brain makes thoughts and feelings. But new studies show that the heart and the brain keep talking to each other all the time, and that heart signals can shape what we feel.
examples: When you are scared, your heart pounds. Is the fear in your heart or your brain?
In many Indian languages, as in English, the word for heart, like 'dil' or 'hriday', is also used for love and courage.
In ancient Egypt, people who prepared a body for burial kept the heart inside it, but took out the brain and threw it away.

perspectives.who: The ancient Egyptians, and Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: The heart is the centre of the person. It is where we think and feel. Aristotle thought the brain's job was to cool the blood.

perspectives.who: Galen, a Greek doctor working in Rome about 1,850 years ago, and most scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Thinking and feeling happen in the brain. The heart is a pump. A person with a new heart from a donor is still the same person, with the same memories and loves.

perspectives.who: Scientists studying how we sense our insides, since about the 2000s
perspectives.explanation: Both are partly right. The brain makes feelings, but it listens to the heart. Signals from each heartbeat travel to the brain. In one experiment, people found scary faces a little scarier when the faces flashed up just as their heart was beating. How much the heart shapes our feelings is still being studied.

explanations.art: A child's outline with a heart and a brain linked by glowing lines going both ways, with small feeling faces floating between them.
explanations.context: This card is about an old question with new answers: does the heart have anything to do with our feelings?

agreed.text: The heart is a muscle pump that pushes blood round the body in a closed loop, and the same blood goes round again and again.
agreed.evidence: William Harvey showed this in 1628. He tied cords around arms and watched veins swell on one side only. He also worked out that the heart pumps far more blood in an hour than a body could make. Today doctors can watch blood flow on ultrasound screens.

agreed.text: We breathe in oxygen, and we breathe out carbon dioxide and water.
agreed.evidence: Breathed-out air turns limewater milky, which shows carbon dioxide. It fogs up a cold mirror, which shows water. Machines in hospitals measure the gases in every breath.

agreed.text: Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs, and red blood cells carry it all over the body.
agreed.evidence: Doctors clip a small light sensor on a fingertip to measure how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Blood from an artery is bright red. Blood from a vein is darker.

agreed.text: Every cell uses oxygen to get energy from food, and makes carbon dioxide as waste.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can measure the oxygen used and carbon dioxide made by single cells in a laboratory. More work means more oxygen used, which is why we breathe harder when we run.

agreed.text: Exercise makes the heart and lungs stronger, and smoke and dirty air harm them.
agreed.evidence: Many large studies, following thousands of people for many years, show that active people have healthier hearts. Studies in Indian cities link smoky, dusty air to more coughs, asthma and lung illness.

challenging.claim: Blood is made fresh in the liver from food, and is used up in the body like fuel. It does not go round.
challenging.who: Galen, a Greek doctor in Rome about 1,850 years ago. Doctors followed his ideas for about 1,400 years.
challenging.for: Galen cut open many animals and was a careful observer. Blood really does carry food, and the body really does use it.
challenging.against: William Harvey measured and counted. A heart pushes out more blood in an hour than the weight of a person. No liver could make that much. So the same blood must go round and round.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what blood does, which doctors believed for a very long time.

challenging.claim: Blood soaks from the right side of the heart to the left side through tiny invisible holes in the wall between them.
challenging.who: Galen, and the doctors who followed him
challenging.for: Blood does get from the right side to the left side somehow. The holes were too small to see, so nobody could prove they were not there.
challenging.against: About 780 years ago, Ibn al-Nafis, a doctor in Cairo, wrote that the wall has no holes at all. He said the blood must go from the right side of the heart to the lungs, mix with air, and come back to the left side. He was right, but his book was forgotten in Europe. It was found again only in 1924.
challenging.context: This card is about how blood gets from one side of the heart to the other, and a doctor who saw the truth centuries early.

challenging.claim: The blood in your veins is blue, and turns red when it touches air.
challenging.who: A very common idea today, even in some old school pictures
challenging.for: Veins really do look blue through skin. Many diagrams colour them blue to show they carry blood low in oxygen.
challenging.against: Blood taken from a vein in a sealed tube, with no air touching it, is dark red. Veins look blue only because of how skin scatters light. The blue in diagrams is a colour code, not the real colour.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common idea: that blood is blue inside us.

challenging.claim: We suck air into our lungs.
challenging.who: How most of us describe breathing
challenging.for: It feels like sucking. You pull your tummy and chest and the air comes in.
challenging.against: You do not pull the air. Your diaphragm moves down and your chest gets bigger. Then the air outside, which is always pressing on everything, pushes itself in to fill the space. That is why you cannot breathe on the Moon, where there is no air to push in.
challenging.context: This card is about how air really gets into your lungs.

challenging.claim: Each animal has a fixed number of heartbeats in its life, about a billion, so a slow heart means a long life.
challenging.who: An idea several scientists have written about since the 1990s
challenging.for: When you multiply heart speed by lifespan, many mammals come out near a billion beats. Small fast-hearted animals often live short lives.
challenging.against: There are many exceptions. Humans get two to three billion beats. Birds live much longer than their fast hearts suggest. Exercise makes your heart beat fast for a while, but makes most people live longer, not shorter.
challenging.context: This card looks at an idea about heartbeats and how long animals live.

challenging.claim: Your heart is on the left side of your chest.
challenging.who: Most people, which is why we put a hand on the left side for a pledge
challenging.for: You feel the beat most strongly on the left, because the bottom tip of the heart points left and taps the chest wall there.
challenging.against: The heart sits almost in the middle, behind the breastbone, tipped a little to the left. In about one person in 10,000, the heart and other organs are flipped, like a mirror picture.
challenging.context: This card is about where the heart really is in your chest.

big_questions.q: Your heart has beaten every second since before you were born. What would it be like if you had to remember to make it beat?
big_questions.hint: Think about sleeping. Who would make it beat then?

big_questions.q: The blood that leaves your heart now will be back in about a minute. Is it the same blood, or is it now different blood?
big_questions.hint: What has it picked up and dropped off on the way?

big_questions.q: Why do you think the lungs need such a huge inside surface, nearly as big as a badminton court, folded into your chest?
big_questions.hint: Think about drying clothes. Do they dry faster folded up or spread out?

big_questions.q: When you breathe out, the carbon dioxide may later go into a neem tree. When the tree gives out oxygen, someone else may breathe it in. Where does your breath end?
big_questions.hint: Follow one breath for a day. Where might it go?

big_questions.q: Some of the air atoms in your next breath were probably breathed by people who lived hundreds of years ago. How does that make you feel about strangers?
big_questions.hint: The air is shared by everyone who has ever lived. Can anyone own it?

big_questions.q: Helen Taussig could hardly hear, so she felt heartbeats with her fingers. What other ways might there be to know something, besides the usual way?
big_questions.hint: Think of a person who is blind reading with their fingers, or a dog smelling who is home.

big_questions.q: Ibn al-Nafis worked out where blood goes 400 years before William Harvey, but Europe forgot him. Who decides whose discoveries are remembered?
big_questions.hint: Think of the language the book was in, and who could read it.

big_questions.q: If your heart is a pump and your lungs are bags of air, where are you? Are you in your heart, your brain, your breath, or everywhere?
big_questions.hint: There is no right answer. What do you feel when you sit very still?

big_questions.q: When you are scared, your heart beats fast, and when your heart beats fast, you can feel scared. Which comes first?
big_questions.hint: Try running on the spot, then sitting still. Does a fast heart feel a little like excitement?

big_questions.q: Plants make the oxygen we breathe, and we make the carbon dioxide plants use. Who is looking after whom?
big_questions.hint: Could plants live without animals? Could animals live without plants?

big_questions.q: A newborn's heart beats about twice as fast as a grown-up's. Why do you think hearts slow down as we grow?
big_questions.hint: Think of the mouse and the elephant. Which beats faster?

story.title: The Doctor Who Listened With Her Fingers
story.note: Real: Helen Taussig (1898 to 1986) lost much of her hearing as a young doctor and learned to feel heartbeats with her fingers. Her idea of a new pipe to the lungs for 'blue babies', the Boston surgeon who turned her down, Alfred Blalock and Vivien Thomas working it out together, Vivien Thomas's lost college savings, Eileen Saxon's operation in November 1944 with Thomas on a stool behind the surgeon, her lips turning pink, and Thomas's honorary degree in 1976 are all real. Imagined: the exact words spoken, the small scenes, and what people thought. For the parent: Eileen lived for some months and then died after a later operation, which the story leaves out. Thousands of children after her grew up because of this operation.
text: In a big hospital in Baltimore, in America, the babies on one ward were blue. Not the blue of the sky. The blue of lips that have stayed too long in cold water. Their fingernails were blue. Their tiny toes were blue. When they cried, they turned bluer still. Then they had to squat down, or lie curled with their knees pulled up, gasping for breath.

The doctor who looked after them was called Helen Taussig. She was a children's heart doctor. It was the early 1940s, and she had a secret that was not really a secret. She could hardly hear. An illness had taken most of her hearing years before. A heart doctor who cannot hear a heartbeat is like a singer who cannot hear a song. So Helen had taught her hands to listen instead.

She would lay her fingers flat on a baby's chest, very gently, and wait. Through her fingertips she felt the heart. She felt the push, and the shudder, and the rush of blood where it should not be. She felt it the way you feel a drum through the floor at a wedding. Other doctors heard a heart. Helen felt one, and she remembered every heart she had ever felt.

Every heart has one simple job. It squeezes, about a hundred times a minute in a baby, and pushes blood along two loops. One loop goes from the heart to the lungs and back. In the lungs, the blood picks up oxygen from the air, and turns bright red. The other loop goes from the heart out to the whole body, where the oxygen is used, and then back again. Round and round go the two circles, joined at the heart.

Helen's blue babies had hearts that were built a little wrong. There was a hole inside, and the doorway to the lungs was far too narrow. So too little blood went to the lungs. Dark blood that had never visited the air went straight back out to the body. That was the blue. The babies were not short of blood. Their blood was short of a journey.

Helen noticed something odd. Some blue babies seemed almost well when they were born. They turned bluer only after a few days or weeks. Why then? She thought about it for a long time. Every baby is born with a small extra pipe beside the heart, a shortcut that closes by itself soon after birth. Perhaps, she thought, in these babies that little pipe had been sending extra blood to the lungs. When it closed, they lost it. And they turned blue.

So the answer was not to mend the whole heart. Nobody in the world could do that yet. The answer was to give the blood a new road to the lungs. Build a new pipe. More blood to the lungs would mean more oxygen. More oxygen would mean pink.

She took her idea to a famous surgeon in Boston. He was not interested. She came home. Then a new surgeon arrived at her own hospital, Dr Alfred Blalock. He listened. And he had someone working beside him called Vivien Thomas.

Vivien Thomas had wanted to be a doctor. He had worked as a carpenter to save money for college. Then the banks crashed, and his savings were gone. He was a Black man in a city that kept Black and white people apart. On paper he was a laboratory helper, paid like a cleaner. But his hands were the most skilful in the building. For months, in the laboratory, he practised the new pipe on animals. He worked out every stitch. The blood vessels he joined were as thin as wet paper.

On a cold day in November 1944, a little girl called Eileen Saxon lay on the operating table. She was more than a year old. But she weighed only as much as a baby of two months. She was very blue. The operation had never been done on a person. Dr Blalock wanted one person beside him more than anyone. He asked Vivien Thomas to stand on a stool, just behind his shoulder, where he could see.

So Vivien stood and watched. Now and then he said quietly, 'That's right,' or 'A little further.' Dr Blalock took the artery that carried blood to Eileen's arm. He turned it and stitched its end onto the artery that led to her lungs. A new road. Helen Taussig stood at the end of the table, watching the child's face.

Then the clamps came off. Blood that had been rushing out to the arm now poured along the new road, into the lungs, into the air. Nobody spoke. Everyone watched Eileen's lips. Slowly, as if someone were pouring colour into her, the blue went out of them. They turned pink.

Soon parents were carrying blue children to Baltimore from all over the country, and then from other countries. Helen felt each small chest with her fingers and decided who could be helped. Vivien trained the surgeons who learned the operation. For many years his name was not written on the papers about it. Much later, in 1976, the university gave him an honorary doctor's degree. His painting now hangs on its walls.

Put your fingers flat on your own chest now. Wait. Feel the push. Somewhere under your hand, two circles of blood are turning, one through the air and one through you. Helen Taussig could not hear that sound. She did not need to. She knew where the blood had to go.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the blue was not about a weak heart or too little blood. It was about where the blood went. Blood only picks up oxygen when it passes through the lungs. Send more blood through the lungs, and the child turns pink. This is the whole idea of the unit: two loops, one through the air and one through the body. The story also quietly asks who gets credit, and shows that there is more than one way to listen.
ask: Why were the babies blue? Where was their blood not going?
Why did a new pipe to the lungs turn Eileen pink?
Helen could hardly hear. How did she find out about hearts anyway?
Vivien Thomas was not called a doctor for many years. Why do you think that was? Was it fair?
Feel your own heartbeat with your fingers, like Helen. What does it feel like?
