experiments.title: The Jumping Heart: does exercise change your pulse?
experiments.question: Does jumping make my heart beat faster? And how quickly does it slow down again?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many times will your heart beat in one minute while you sit still? Will it go up or down after one minute of jumping? Write your guesses down.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, count the same way every time. Use the same fingers on the same wrist, and count for exactly 30 seconds with a clock. Sit still for 2 minutes before the first count, so your heart is really resting. Count each time 2 times, because one count can be a mistake.
results_table: Bigger of the two, doubled: beats in 1 minute

materials.item: a clock, watch or phone that shows seconds
a pencil and the results table
a soft space to jump, like a mat or a rug

experiments.safety: If your child has a heart condition or asthma, ask your doctor before the jumping part. Stop at once if anyone feels dizzy, sick or has chest pain. Jump on a mat, not a slippery floor.

schedule.what: Guess. Count your pulse sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after two minutes of rest. Make a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each time you counted. Make each bar as tall as the beats in one minute.
experiments.context: This is the jumping heart experiment. You count your heartbeats at your wrist while sitting still, then just after jumping, then after a rest. You find out how exercise changes your heart.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: heartbeats in one minute
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with two fingers on the thumb side of the other wrist, a clock with a second hand beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 2 minutes. Then count your pulse for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The same child doing star jumps on a rug, arms and legs wide.
setup.caption: 2. Do star jumps for 1 minute.

setup.art: The child sitting again, quickly finding the wrist pulse, slightly out of breath, the clock beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Count again straight away. Then rest 2 minutes and count once more.

flow.do: 1. Sit together. 2. Show your child where to press: two fingers, not the thumb, on the thumb side of the inside of the wrist. 3. If it is hard to find, try the side of the neck, just under the jaw. Press gently.
flow.say: Your heart squeezes blood into tubes called arteries. Each squeeze makes the tube bulge. You can feel the bulge with your fingers. That's your pulse. Let's find it. Two fingers here, gently. Not your thumb, because your thumb has its own pulse.
flow.kid: Put two fingers on your wrist, on the thumb side. Press gently. Can you feel little taps? That is your pulse. Each tap is one heartbeat.
flow.parent: It can take a minute to find. Move the fingers about a little and press softer, not harder. The neck pulse is easier for many children. Never press on both sides of the neck at once.

ask.q: What do you feel under your fingers?

flow.context: This is the first step of the jumping heart experiment. Here you learn to find your pulse.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to write down their guesses. 2. Sit still for 2 minutes. 3. Say 'Go' and count beats for exactly 30 seconds. 4. Write the number down. 5. Do it again for a second count.
flow.say: First, guess. Then we sit very still for two minutes, so your heart is resting. When I say go, count every tap until I say stop. That's 30 seconds.
flow.kid: Guess first. Then sit still for two minutes. When the grown-up says go, count each tap. Stop when they say stop. Write the number down.
flow.parent: Children often lose count. That is why we count twice. If the two counts are very different, count a third time. To get beats in one minute, double the 30-second count. For example, 44 beats in 30 seconds means 88 beats in one minute.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

check.q: You counted 45 beats in 30 seconds. How many beats is that in one whole minute?
check.why: One minute is two lots of 30 seconds. So you double 45. 45 + 45 = 90. Picking 45 usually means forgetting that we only counted for half a minute. Picking 30 mixes up the seconds with the beats.

flow.do: 1. Your child does star jumps for 1 minute. 2. As soon as they stop, they sit and find their pulse. 3. Count for 30 seconds. 4. Write it down. Count only once here, because the heart slows down fast.
flow.say: Now let's make your muscles work. Star jumps for one minute! Go! Stop! Quick, find your pulse. Count!
flow.kid: Do star jumps for one minute. Stop. Quickly find your pulse. Count for 30 seconds. Write it down.
flow.parent: Be quick to start counting, because the heart begins to slow straight away. Expect the count to be much higher, perhaps half as much again or nearly double. Notice the breathing too.

ask.q: What else changed when you jumped, apart from your pulse?

flow.do: 1. Rest for 2 minutes, sitting still. 2. Count for 30 seconds again. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Now rest for two minutes. Let's see how fast your heart comes back down.
flow.kid: Sit and rest for two minutes. Then count your pulse again. Is it back to normal yet?
flow.think: A fit heart slows down quickly after exercise. Why do you think that might be?

flow.do: Help your child turn the numbers into a bar chart: one bar for sitting still, one for just after jumping, one for after the rest.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each count. The taller the bar, the faster your heart was beating.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each time you counted. A taller bar means a faster heart.

chart.title: Made-up example results: heartbeats in one minute
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: Look at the bar chart. Which bar is tallest?
options: Sitting still
Just after jumping
After 2 minutes of rest
check.why: Just after jumping, the muscles were working hard and needed lots of oxygen, so the heart beat fastest. Picking 'after rest' usually means thinking the heart keeps speeding up after you stop. In fact it starts slowing down straight away.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: jumping makes my heart beat faster. What I saw: sitting still it was 88 beats a minute, after jumping it was 148, and after resting it went down to 102. Why: my muscles needed more oxygen to jump, so my heart pumped blood faster to bring it.

experiments.title: The Milky Breath: is breathed-out air different?
experiments.question: Is the air I breathe out the same as the air in the room?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Air goes into you and comes out again. Do you think it comes out the same, or changed? What might be different?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two glasses with the same amount of limewater. Push room air through one and breathed-out air through the other, for the same time. Only the kind of air changes.
results_table: What it looked like after 1 minute

materials.item: chuna, the edible white lime paste sold for paan, about half a teaspoon
a jug of water and two clear glasses
two drinking straws
a balloon or an empty squeezy bottle, to push room air
a steel plate kept in the fridge for 10 minutes

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the chuna. It can sting eyes and skin. Wash hands after touching it. Never drink limewater. When blowing through the straw, only blow out. Never suck up.

schedule.what: A grown-up makes the limewater and leaves it to settle overnight. Do the cold plate breath test.
Pour off the clear limewater. Push room air through one glass and blow your breath through the other. Compare.

experiments.record: Draw the two glasses after one minute. Write what was different. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.
experiments.context: This is the milky breath experiment. Limewater is clear water that goes cloudy when carbon dioxide bubbles through it. You test whether the air you breathe out has more carbon dioxide than room air.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a little white chuna paste into a jug of water, then a jug left with a white layer settled at the bottom and clear water on top.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stirs chuna into water. Leave it overnight. Pour off the clear part.

setup.art: Two clear glasses of limewater side by side; a squeezy bottle pushing room air through a straw into one, a child gently blowing through a straw into the other.
setup.caption: 2. Push room air into one glass. Blow your breath gently into the other.

setup.art: The same two glasses after a minute: the room-air one still clear, the breath one milky white.
setup.caption: 3. Watch which glass turns milky.

flow.do: 1. Take the steel plate out of the fridge. 2. Ask your child to breathe out slowly onto it from close up. 3. Look at the mist.
flow.say: Breathe out onto this cold plate. What do you see? That mist is water. So breathed-out air carries water out of you.
flow.kid: Breathe out onto the cold plate. Do you see a mist? That mist is water from inside you.

ask.q: Where did the water come from?

flow.context: This is the first step of the milky breath experiment. A cold plate shows that breathed-out air carries water.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up stirs half a teaspoon of chuna into a full jug of water. 2. Leave it overnight, without stirring.
flow.say: Chuna is lime, the same paste used in paan. In water it makes limewater. Limewater has a trick. It turns milky when a gas called carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
flow.kid: A grown-up stirs chuna into water. You leave it overnight. Tomorrow it will be clear, with white stuff at the bottom.
flow.parent: Chuna is slaked lime, which is calcium hydroxide. It is mildly caustic, so keep it away from eyes and wash your hands. Settled limewater looks like clear water. Only the clear top part is used.

flow.do: 1. Carefully pour the clear limewater off the top into two glasses, the same amount in each. 2. Put a straw in each. 3. Squeeze room air through the first straw with the squeezy bottle, 20 squeezes. 4. Your child blows gently through the second straw for about one minute, taking breaths in through the nose.
flow.say: In this glass we push ordinary room air. In this glass you blow your breath out. Blow gently, only out, never suck. Watch both glasses.
flow.kid: Watch the two glasses. The grown-up pushes room air into one. You blow gently into the other. Only blow out. Never suck.
flow.parent: The breath glass usually turns milky within a minute. The room-air glass stays clear, or goes cloudy only very slowly, because room air has very little carbon dioxide.

check.q: The glass you breathed into turned milky. The room-air glass stayed clear. What does that tell us?
options: Breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide than room air
Breath has dirt in it
The straw was dirty
check.why: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide goes through it. Your breath turned it milky fast, so your breath has much more carbon dioxide than room air. Your cells made that carbon dioxide when they used food for energy. Picking 'dirt' usually means thinking breath is dusty. But the milky white is a new substance made when carbon dioxide meets the lime.

flow.do: Ask your child where the carbon dioxide came from.
flow.say: Where do you think this gas came from? It wasn't in the room air. So it must have been made inside you.
flow.kid: The gas was not in the room air. So where did it come from?

ask.q: Where did the carbon dioxide come from?
good: My cells made it when they used food.

flow.think: Plants take in carbon dioxide. Could a plant use your breath?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the air I breathe out is different from room air. What I saw: my breath turned limewater milky, but room air did not, and my breath fogged the cold plate. Why: my body uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water, and I breathe them out.

experiments.title: How Big Is One Breath? The upside-down bottle
experiments.question: How much air do I push out in one ordinary breath? And in my biggest breath?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will one ordinary breath fill a small cup, a big bottle or a bucket? Will your biggest breath be bigger than a grown-up's?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, everyone uses the same bottle and blows out through the same kind of tube. Each person has their own tube, to keep it clean. Do each kind of breath 2 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a clear 2-litre plastic bottle with a cap
a measuring jug
a marker pen and tape
a bucket or big tub of water
a bendy tube, about 50 cm, or several bendy straws joined, one for each person

experiments.safety: Each person uses their own tube. Wipe up spilled water, so nobody slips. Stop if anyone feels dizzy from big breaths, and sit down.

schedule.what: Mark the bottle every 100 ml. Fill it and turn it upside down in the bucket. Blow ordinary and biggest breaths. Read the air space. Compare with the family.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each person's biggest breath.
experiments.context: This is the upside-down bottle experiment. A bottle full of water stands upside down in a bucket. When you blow into it through a tube, air pushes the water out, and you can read how much air you breathed out.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: biggest breath out
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Yours will be different.

setup.art: A child pouring 100 ml from a measuring jug into a plastic bottle and drawing a line on tape at the water level, several lines already marked.
setup.caption: 1. Pour in water 100 ml at a time. Mark a line each time.

setup.art: A full bottle held upside down with its neck under the water in a bucket, a bendy tube poking up into its neck.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle. Turn it upside down in the bucket. Push a tube into its neck.

setup.art: A child blowing into the tube, a big air space at the top of the upside-down bottle, a line showing the air reaching the 1,500 ml mark.
setup.caption: 3. Breathe out through the tube. Read how far the air pushed the water down.

flow.do: 1. Stick a strip of tape down the side of the bottle. 2. Pour in 100 ml of water with the jug. 3. Hold the bottle upside down, so the water is at the cap end, and mark the level. 4. Repeat, 100 ml at a time, until full.
flow.say: We're turning this bottle into a breath measurer. We'll mark a line for every 100 millilitres of water. Hold it upside down each time, because that's how we will use it.
flow.kid: Pour 100 ml of water in. Turn the bottle upside down. Mark the water line on the tape. Do it again and again until it is full.
flow.parent: Marking with the bottle upside down matters, because the bottle's shape is different at each end. Numbering every 500 ml mark in big writing makes reading easier.
flow.context: This is the first step of the upside-down bottle experiment. Here you turn a bottle into a tool for measuring breath.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the top and screw on the cap. 2. Turn it upside down with the neck under the water in the bucket. 3. Unscrew the cap under the water. 4. Hold the bottle still and push the end of the tube into its neck.
flow.say: Now the tricky bit. Upside down, neck under water, take the cap off under the water. The water stays in! Air is pressing on the water in the bucket and holds it up.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle. Put the cap on. Turn it upside down in the bucket. Take the cap off under the water. Push the tube into the neck.
flow.parent: A grown-up holds the bottle steady. If air gets in while setting up, start again.

flow.do: 1. Your child breathes in normally, then breathes out normally through the tube, once. 2. Read the mark at the bottom of the air space. 3. Refill and set up again. 4. Now take the biggest breath in they can, and blow out all of it. 5. Read the mark. Do the biggest breath 2 times.
flow.say: First an ordinary, everyday breath out. Just a normal one. Then refill, and do your biggest ever breath in, and blow it all out.
flow.kid: Breathe out one normal breath into the tube. Read the line. Then take your biggest breath. Blow it all out. Read the line again.
flow.parent: An ordinary breath for an 8-year-old is often 150 to 300 ml. The biggest breath out may be 1,000 to 2,000 ml. Grown-ups' biggest breaths may be bigger than the bottle. If so, write 'more than 2,000 ml'.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

check.q: An ordinary breath out pushed the water down to the 200 ml line. Your biggest breath reached 1,500 ml. Which is true?
options: You use only a small part of your lungs in an ordinary breath
Your lungs are full of water
An ordinary breath uses all your lungs
check.why: Your biggest breath was more than 7 times your ordinary one. So most of the time you only use a small part of what your lungs can hold. The rest is spare, ready for running and shouting. Picking 'uses all your lungs' usually means thinking every breath is as big as it can be.

flow.do: Test other family members with their own tubes. Make a bar chart of everyone's biggest breath.
flow.say: Now let's test the family. Everyone gets their own tube. Who do you think has the biggest breath?
flow.kid: Test your family. Each person uses their own tube. Draw a bar for each person's biggest breath.
flow.think: People who live high in the mountains of Ladakh, or who sing or play the shehnai, often have big breaths. Why might that be?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: one ordinary breath is quite small, but my lungs can hold much more. What I saw: my ordinary breath was 200 ml and my biggest was 1,500 ml. Why: my diaphragm and ribs can make my chest much bigger when I really try.

activities.title: Laennec's Paper Tube: make a stethoscope

materials.item: a sheet of thick paper or a notebook cover
tape
a kitchen funnel and about 50 cm of plastic tube that fits it, for the better version

activities.safety: Never put the tube inside anyone's ear. Hold it just at the opening. Never shout or tap into it.

schedule.what: Make a paper tube stethoscope and a funnel stethoscope. Listen to a heartbeat with each.

activities.record: Write the sound you heard in letters, like 'lub-dub'. Draw where on the chest it was loudest.
activities.context: In this activity you make a stethoscope, the doctor's listening tool, first from rolled-up paper like the very first one in 1816, and then from a funnel and a tube.

setup.art: Hands rolling a sheet of paper into a tight tube and taping it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll paper into a tight tube. Tape it.

setup.art: A child with the end of the paper tube at their ear, the other end resting on a grown-up's chest, a little left of the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Rest one end on the chest. Put your ear at the other end.

setup.art: A kitchen funnel joined to a plastic tube, the funnel held flat on a chest and the tube end near a child's ear.
setup.caption: 3. Try a funnel and tube. Is it louder?

flow.do: Tell the story of the first stethoscope.
flow.say: In 1816 a French doctor called René Laennec had a patient with a sore chest. Doctors then put their ear right on the chest to listen. He felt that was awkward. So he rolled up some paper into a tube, put one end on her chest and the other at his ear. He heard the heart louder and clearer than ever before. That was the first stethoscope.
flow.kid: Long ago, a doctor named Laennec rolled up paper into a tube. He used it to listen to a heart. It worked! Let's make one.
flow.context: This is the first step of the stethoscope activity. You hear how the first stethoscope was invented, from rolled-up paper.

flow.do: 1. Roll the paper into a tight tube, about as wide as a coin. 2. Tape it. 3. In a quiet room, rest one end on the grown-up's chest, a little left of the middle. 4. Your child puts their ear gently against the other end.
flow.say: Put the tube here, a little to the left of the middle of my chest. Now ear to the other end. Shh. What can you hear?
flow.kid: Roll the paper into a tube. Put one end on a grown-up's chest. Put your ear to the other end. Be very quiet. Listen.

ask.q: What does it sound like? Say it in letters.

flow.parent: Turn off the fan for this. The two sounds are the valves, the little flap doors in the heart, snapping shut.

flow.do: 1. Push the plastic tube onto the funnel spout. 2. Hold the funnel flat on the chest. 3. Your child holds the open end of the tube at the opening of their ear. 4. Try different places on the chest. 5. Then listen to the chest while the grown-up breathes in deeply.
flow.say: Now the funnel. It catches more sound. Move it around. Where is the heartbeat loudest? Now listen while I take a deep breath.
flow.kid: Hold the tube end at your ear. Do not push it in. Move the funnel around. Where is the heartbeat loudest? Listen to a deep breath too.

check.q: Why does the funnel stethoscope sound louder than just your ear in the air?
options: The funnel catches the sound from a wide patch and the tube carries it to your ear
The funnel makes new sounds
The tube has a battery
check.why: Sound from the heart spreads out through the chest. The wide funnel catches it from a big patch, and the tube carries it straight to your ear without spreading out again. Picking 'makes new sounds' usually means thinking the tool adds the sound. It only collects it.

flow.think: Helen Taussig could hardly hear, so she felt heartbeats with her fingers. Can you feel one with your hand flat on someone's chest?

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a body outline and mark where the beat was loudest.
flow.say: Show me on this drawing where the heartbeat was loudest.
flow.kid: Draw a body. Mark where the heartbeat was loudest.
flow.parent: It is usually loudest just left of the breastbone, a little below the middle of the chest. The heart sits almost in the middle, with its tip pointing left.

activities.title: The Bottle Lung: a model of breathing

materials.item: a small plastic bottle, about 500 ml
two balloons
a rubber band and tape
scissors, for a grown-up

activities.safety: Only a grown-up cuts the bottle. Cover the cut edge with tape, because it can be sharp.

schedule.what: Build the bottle lung. Pull the bottom balloon to make the lung balloon fill.

activities.record: Draw the bottle lung twice: once with the bottom pulled down, once pushed up. Label the lung, the windpipe and the diaphragm.
activities.context: In this activity you build a model of breathing from a bottle and two balloons. The bottle is the chest, one balloon is a lung, and a stretched balloon at the bottom is the diaphragm, the breathing muscle.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting the bottom off a small plastic bottle, and taping the cut edge.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom off the bottle.

setup.art: A balloon hanging inside the bottle from its neck, held by a rubber band, and a second balloon, knotted and cut, stretched over the open bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Hang one balloon inside the neck. Stretch the other across the bottom.

setup.art: A hand pulling the knot of the bottom balloon down, and the balloon inside the bottle puffing up.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the bottom down. Watch the lung balloon fill.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom off the bottle and tapes the edge. 2. Push one balloon into the neck, with its mouth stretched over the top of the bottle. Hold it with a rubber band. 3. Tie a knot in the second balloon and cut off its round end. 4. Stretch the rest across the open bottom of the bottle, with the knot hanging down. Tape it.
flow.say: The bottle is your chest. The balloon inside is a lung. The neck is your windpipe. And this stretchy balloon at the bottom is your diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs.
flow.kid: The bottle is your chest. The inside balloon is a lung. The bottom balloon is your breathing muscle. Help build it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bottle lung activity. You build a breathing model from a bottle and two balloons.

flow.do: 1. Your child pulls the knot down gently and watches the inside balloon. 2. Then they push it up. 3. Do it slowly, then fast.
flow.say: Pull the knot down. What happens to the lung? Now push it up. You're breathing for the bottle!
flow.kid: Pull the knot down. The lung balloon fills! Push it up. It empties. You are making the bottle breathe.

check.q: When you pull the bottom balloon down, the lung balloon fills up. Why?
options: Pulling down makes more room inside, and air from outside pushes in
The bottom balloon blows air into it
The lung balloon pulls air in by itself
check.why: Pulling the bottom down makes the space inside the bottle bigger. Air from outside then pushes in through the neck and fills the balloon. Your diaphragm does the same. Picking 'the lung pulls air in by itself' is a very common idea. But lungs have no muscles. They fill because the chest makes room.

ask.q: Which part of the model is your diaphragm?
good: The stretchy balloon at the bottom.

flow.do: Ask your child to put one hand on their tummy and one on the bottle, and breathe in time with the model.
flow.say: Put a hand on your tummy. Breathe in as you pull the knot down. Breathe out as you push it up. Can you feel your own diaphragm doing the same thing?
flow.kid: Hand on your tummy. Breathe in as you pull down. Breathe out as you push up. Can you feel your own breathing muscle?
flow.think: In what ways is the model not like a real chest? Real lungs have ribs around them, and there are two of them.

activities.title: Squeeze Like a Heart

materials.item: a soft rubber ball, a tennis ball or a wet sponge
a clock that shows seconds

schedule.what: Squeeze a ball once every second for one minute. Feel how hard your heart works.

activities.record: Write how many squeezes you managed, and how your hand felt after one minute.
activities.context: In this activity you squeeze a ball as often as your heart beats, to feel how hard your heart works all day and all night.

setup.art: A child's hand gripping a tennis ball tightly.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a ball in one hand.

setup.art: The same hand squeezing the ball, a clock beside it, small motion lines.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze hard once every second for one minute.

setup.art: The child shaking out a tired hand, a heart beside them still beating.
setup.caption: 3. Feel your tired hand. Your heart never stops.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the ball. 2. Watch the clock. 3. Say 'squeeze' once every second for one minute, while they squeeze hard each time.
flow.say: Your heart squeezes about once a second, every second of your life. Let's see what that feels like. Squeeze hard each time I say squeeze.
flow.kid: Squeeze the ball hard each time you hear 'squeeze'. Keep going for one minute. Like your heart!

ask.q: How does your hand feel now?

flow.context: This is the squeeze like a heart activity. You squeeze a ball once a second for a minute, the way your heart squeezes.

flow.do: Talk about how the heart never gets tired like this.
flow.say: Your hand got tired in one minute. Your heart has done this since before you were born, about 100,000 times every day. Heart muscle is a special kind. It rests for a tiny moment after every single beat, and it has its own big supply of blood.
flow.kid: Your hand got tired fast. Your heart squeezes all day and all night. It rests a tiny bit after every beat. It has been doing this all your life.

check.q: Your hand got tired after one minute of squeezing. Why doesn't your heart get tired the same way?
options: Heart muscle is special: it rests between every beat and has lots of blood bringing it oxygen
The heart only beats when you are awake
The heart doesn't really squeeze
check.why: Heart muscle is different from arm muscle. After each squeeze it relaxes for a moment, and its own blood vessels keep bringing it plenty of oxygen. Picking 'only when awake' is not right. Your heart beats in your sleep too, only a bit slower.

flow.think: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day. How many times has it beaten since you woke up today?

activities.title: The Pulse Watcher: see your heartbeat

materials.item: a small ball of atta dough or modelling clay, the size of a pea
a toothpick or a matchstick with its head cut off

activities.safety: Use a toothpick with a blunted tip. Do not use a match with a head on it.

schedule.what: Stand a toothpick in dough on your wrist pulse. Watch it tick. Count the ticks.

activities.record: Draw your wrist with the pulse watcher on it. Write how many ticks you counted in 30 seconds.
activities.context: In this activity you stand a toothpick in a little ball of dough on your wrist, right over your pulse. Each heartbeat makes it tick, so you can see your heart beating.

setup.art: Fingers finding the pulse on the thumb side of a wrist.
setup.caption: 1. Find your pulse on your wrist.

setup.art: A pea-sized ball of dough with a toothpick standing in it, placed on that spot.
setup.caption: 2. Put the dough ball there. Stand the toothpick up in it.

setup.art: A close-up of the toothpick leaning a tiny bit one way, then back, with small tick marks.
setup.caption: 3. Keep your arm still. Watch the toothpick tick.

flow.do: 1. Rest your child's arm flat on a table, palm up. 2. Find the pulse. 3. Press the dough ball gently onto that spot. 4. Stand the toothpick straight up in it. 5. Keep the arm very still.
flow.say: Watch the toothpick. Every little tick is your heart pushing blood into the artery under it.
flow.kid: Rest your arm on the table, palm up. Put the dough ball on your pulse. Stand the toothpick in it. Keep still. Watch it tick!
flow.parent: It may take a few tries to find the right spot. Move the dough a little if the toothpick does not tick.

ask.q: Is the ticking steady, like a clock?
good: It goes a bit faster sometimes.

flow.context: This is the pulse watcher activity. A toothpick on your wrist ticks with every heartbeat.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks for 30 seconds. 2. Then ask your child to take a slow, deep breath in, and watch. 3. Then a long slow breath out.
flow.say: Count the ticks for 30 seconds. Now breathe in slowly and watch. Now breathe out slowly. Do the ticks change?
flow.kid: Count the ticks for 30 seconds. Now breathe in slowly. Then out slowly. Do the ticks change speed?

check.q: The toothpick ticks once every heartbeat. What is making it move?
options: The artery under the skin bulging each time the heart pushes blood
Your muscles twitching
The wind
check.why: Each squeeze of the heart sends a push of blood along the artery. The artery bulges a tiny bit and lifts the dough. That is your pulse. Picking 'muscles twitching' is a fair guess, but your arm muscles are relaxed. The tick matches your heartbeat exactly.

flow.think: Many people's heart speeds up a tiny bit on the breath in, and slows a tiny bit on the breath out. Did yours?

activities.title: Cooling Cloud: slow breath, slow heart

materials.item: a clock that shows seconds
a quiet place to sit

activities.safety: Breathe gently. If your child feels dizzy, stop and breathe normally.

schedule.what: Count your pulse. Breathe in for 4 and out for 6, ten times. Count your pulse again.

activities.record: Write your pulse before and after the slow breathing. Draw how you felt before and after.
activities.context: In this activity you count your pulse, then do slow breathing, breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6, and count again. You find out whether slow breathing can calm your heart.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged with two fingers on the wrist and a clock nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Count your pulse for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The child with one hand on the belly, eyes closed, a cloud shape growing as they breathe in and shrinking as they blow out.
setup.caption: 2. Breathe in for 4. Blow out slowly for 6, like cooling hot soup.

setup.art: The child counting the pulse again, looking calm.
setup.caption: 3. After ten slow breaths, count your pulse again.

flow.do: 1. Sit together on the floor. 2. Count your child's pulse for 30 seconds and write it down.
flow.say: First, let's count your pulse as it is now.
flow.kid: Sit down. Count your pulse for 30 seconds. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the cooling cloud activity. You count your pulse before some slow breathing.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put one hand on their belly. 2. Count slowly: in 2, 3, 4. Out, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. 3. Do this ten times.
flow.say: Hand on your belly. Breathe in through your nose, 2, 3, 4. Feel your belly rise like a cloud. Now blow out slowly through your mouth, like cooling hot soup, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
flow.kid: Hand on your belly. Breathe in for 4. Feel it rise. Blow out slowly for 6, like cooling hot soup. Do it ten times.
flow.parent: This is the founder's 'Cooling Cloud' breath. The long breath out is the important part. It gently slows the heart through a nerve that runs from the brain to the heart.

flow.do: Count the pulse again for 30 seconds, and compare.
flow.say: Let's count again. Is it the same, faster or slower?
flow.kid: Count your pulse again. Is it the same, faster or slower than before?

check.q: After slow breathing, many people's pulse goes down a little. Why might that be?
options: Long, slow breaths out send a calming message to the heart
Breathing slowly stops the heart
Your fingers got tired
check.why: Your heart and breath are linked by nerves. Each long breath out gives the heart a small 'slow down' message. Picking 'stops the heart' is not right: the heart keeps its own beat and only changes speed a little. If your pulse did not drop, that is fine too. It was already calm.

flow.think: When you feel angry or scared, what could you do with your breath?

activities.title: A Jar of Blood (made from the kitchen)

materials.item: a clear glass jar or glass
water with a tiny pinch of haldi, to make it pale yellow
a cup of rajma, the red kidney beans, uncooked
one white chana or white bean
a pinch of til, sesame seeds

activities.safety: Use uncooked beans only to look at, and do not eat them raw. Small children should not put beans in their nose or mouth.

schedule.what: Build a model of blood in a jar. Use rajma for red cells, chana for white cells, til for platelets and yellow water for plasma.

activities.record: Draw your jar and label the four parts of blood. Write one job for each.
activities.context: In this activity you make a model of blood in a jar from kitchen things. It shows the four parts of blood and how much of each there is.

setup.art: A clear jar half full of pale yellow water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a jar halfway with pale yellow water. This is plasma.

setup.art: A child pouring red rajma beans into the jar until it is nearly half beans.
setup.caption: 2. Add rajma beans until the jar is almost half beans. These are red cells.

setup.art: The jar with one white chana and a few sesame seeds on top of the beans.
setup.caption: 3. Add just one white chana and a pinch of til. Then look at the mix.

flow.do: 1. Pour pale yellow water into the jar until it is about half full. 2. Add rajma until the beans fill nearly half of the jar. 3. Add one white chana. 4. Sprinkle in a pinch of til.
flow.say: Blood looks like just a red liquid. But it's really a crowd of tiny things floating in a yellow liquid. Let's build it. The yellow water is plasma. The rajma are red blood cells. The single chana is a white blood cell. The til seeds are platelets.
flow.kid: Pour yellow water into the jar. That is plasma. Add lots of rajma. They are red blood cells. Add one chana. That is a white blood cell. Sprinkle a little til. They are platelets.
flow.parent: In real blood, a little under half is red cells and a little over half is plasma. For every 600 or so red cells, there is about one white cell. That is why there is only one chana.
flow.context: This is the jar of blood activity. You make a model of blood from yellow water, rajma, one chana and til.

flow.do: Go through the job of each part.
flow.say: The red cells carry oxygen. The plasma carries food and water. The white cell fights germs. The platelets stick together to plug a cut.
flow.kid: Red cells carry oxygen. Plasma carries food and water. White cells fight germs. Platelets plug cuts.

check.q: Why are there so many rajma beans and only one chana in our blood jar?
options: Blood has hundreds of red cells for every white cell
White cells are bigger, so we need fewer
We ran out of chana
check.why: In real blood, red cells are by far the biggest crowd. There are about 600 red cells for every white cell. That is because every part of your body needs oxygen all the time. White cells are only needed where germs get in. Picking 'white cells are bigger' is partly true, they are a bit bigger, but that is not why there are fewer.

flow.do: Leave the jar still for a minute and watch the beans sink.
flow.say: Look. The beans sink to the bottom and the yellow stays on top. Real blood does this too, if it stands in a tube for a long time. The red cells sink, and the yellow plasma stays on top.
flow.kid: Leave the jar still. Watch the beans sink. Real blood does this too, if it stands still in a tube.
flow.think: Why do you think your blood doesn't settle like this inside you?

games.title: The Great Circle: a red blood cell board game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: The Great Circle board: a figure-of-eight path of 24 squares
items: Valve door squares: you may only go forward

printables.title: Tokens to cut out
items: 10 food tokens marked with a roti
4 red blood cell counters, one for each player

printables.title: 20 body cards to cut out
items: You are running! Move 2 extra squares.
You are asleep. Move only 1 square this turn.
Smoky air near a burning rubbish heap. At the lungs this time, pick up only 1 oxygen.
Deep breath in the fresh air of a park. Pick up 1 extra oxygen at the lungs.
A valve snapped shut behind you. Lub-dub! You cannot go backwards.
The leg muscles are working hard. Drop 1 extra oxygen there if you have it.
You scraped your knee. A platelet helps plug it. Miss one turn while it heals.
Climbing stairs to the third floor. Move 2 extra squares.
You had a glass of water. Move 1 extra square.
Scared by a barking dog! Your heart speeds up. Move 2 extra squares.
Slow breathing time. Move 1 square, then take a slow breath with everyone.
Brain needs oxygen to think. Drop 1 oxygen at the brain if you pass it.
Lunch time! Pick up 1 food token at the tummy stop.
Long road to the toes. Move back 1 square, but then never backwards again.
QUESTION: Which side of the heart sends blood to the lungs? Answer right, move 2.
QUESTION: What gas do the leg muscles give you to carry away? Answer right, move 2.
QUESTION: What makes the lub-dub sound? Answer right, move 2.
QUESTION: Where does your blood pick up oxygen? Answer right, move 2.
QUESTION: Why do you breathe faster when you run? Answer right, move 2.
QUESTION: Name one way to keep your lungs healthy. Answer right, move 2.

rules: Each player is a red blood cell. Put all the counters on HEART, RIGHT SIDE.
Take turns. Roll a dice and move forward. Arrows show the way. You can never go backwards, because valves stop you.
When you pass through the lungs, pick up 2 oxygen tokens and drop all your carbon dioxide tokens there.
When you pass a body stop, like the brain or the legs, drop 1 oxygen token there and pick up 1 carbon dioxide token. Each oxygen you deliver scores 1 point.
If you land on a card square, take a body card and do what it says.
You can carry at most 4 oxygen tokens, the way a real red cell can carry only so much.
When every player has gone round the circle 3 times, count your points. The most oxygen delivered wins.
games.context: The Great Circle is a board game where each player is a red blood cell. You carry oxygen from the lungs to the body, and carry carbon dioxide back.

setup.art: A printed figure-of-eight board on the floor, a heart in the middle, pink lungs at the top loop and body stops on the bottom loop.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the board. Put the red cell counters on the right side of the heart.

setup.art: Small paper tokens in three piles: O for oxygen, CO2 for carbon dioxide, and little rotis for food.
setup.caption: 2. Make three piles of tokens.

setup.art: A child moving a red counter past the lungs and picking up two O tokens.
setup.caption: 3. Roll, move, pick up oxygen at the lungs and drop it at body stops.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board on the floor. 2. Put the tokens in three piles. 3. Shuffle the body cards. 4. Everyone puts their red cell counter on HEART, RIGHT SIDE.
flow.say: In this game, you are a red blood cell. Your job is to carry oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body. The heart pushes you round and round.
flow.kid: You are a red blood cell! Put your counter on the right side of the heart. Your job is to carry oxygen to the body.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Great Circle, a board game where you play a red blood cell. Here you set up the board.

flow.do: Play the first trip slowly together. Follow one counter from the heart to the lungs and back.
flow.say: Look. From the right side of the heart, we go first to the lungs. Pick up two oxygen tokens here. Then back to the heart, the left side. Now the heart pushes us out to the body.
flow.kid: Move from the heart to the lungs. Pick up 2 oxygen. Then go back to the heart. Then out to the body!

check.q: In The Great Circle, you are a red blood cell leaving the right side of the heart. Where do you go first?
options: To the lungs, to pick up oxygen
Straight to the legs
To the tummy
check.why: The right side of the heart sends blood to the lungs first, to pick up oxygen. Then it comes back to the left side, which sends it to the body. Picking 'straight to the legs' usually means picturing one big loop. In fact there are two loops, joined at the heart.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling and moving. 2. Pick up and drop tokens as the rules say. 3. Read body cards out loud and do what they say.
flow.say: Every time you drop oxygen at a body stop, tell us what that part will do with it.
flow.kid: Take turns. Roll and move. Drop oxygen at the brain and legs. Pick up carbon dioxide. Read the cards out loud.
flow.parent: Good answers when dropping oxygen: the leg muscles use it to get energy for running, the brain uses it to think. When a player drops carbon dioxide at the lungs, ask: 'What happens to it now?' (We breathe it out.)

ask.q: Why do you drop your carbon dioxide at the lungs?
good: So we can breathe it out.
Because the lungs swap it for oxygen.

flow.do: When a 'You are running!' or 'Scared!' card comes up, stop and do it for real: run on the spot for 20 seconds and feel your heart.
flow.say: This card says we're running. Let's all run on the spot for 20 seconds. Now feel your heart. Is it pushing you round faster?
flow.kid: Run on the spot for 20 seconds. Feel your heart. It pushes the blood round faster when you run.

check.q: The 'You are running!' card lets you move extra squares. Why is that like real life?
options: When you run, the heart pumps faster, so blood goes round faster
Running makes your blood thinner
Red cells have legs
check.why: When you run, your muscles need oxygen faster. So the heart beats faster and harder, and the blood goes round more quickly. Picking 'thinner blood' is a guess many people make, but blood does not get thinner. It just moves faster.

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's points. 2. Then talk about the game.
flow.say: Count your oxygen points. Now think. In real life, your red blood cells go round about once every minute. How many trips would that be in a day?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who delivered the most oxygen? Real red cells go round about once a minute, all day long!
flow.think: A real red blood cell goes round the body about a thousand times a day, for about four months. Then a new one takes its place. Is the you of today made of the same blood as the you of last year?

games.title: Chalk Heart Relay
games.players: 2 to 6 players, outside or in a big room

printables.title: 10 caller cards
items: WALKING TO THE SHOP: walk fast
SLOW BREATHING: stop and take 3 slow breaths, then walk
SMOKY AIR: carry only 1 ball this trip
FRESH AIR IN A PARK: carry 3 balls this trip

printables.title: Deliveries in 1 minute
items: Number of oxygen balls delivered in 1 minute

rules: Draw a big figure of eight on the ground with chalk. Mark a heart where the loops cross, lungs at the top loop and a body basket at the bottom loop.
Put a pile of scrunched-up paper balls at the lungs. These are oxygen.
Players are red blood cells. Each trip, they pick up 2 oxygen balls at the lungs, go back through the heart and drop them in the body basket.
They must always go the same way round, through the heart in the middle each time.
The caller draws a card every minute. The card says how fast to move.
Count how many balls reach the body basket in each minute. Write it on the score sheet.
games.context: The Chalk Heart Relay is a running game where children are red blood cells. They carry paper oxygen balls round a chalk figure of eight, from the lungs to the body, as fast as the body needs.

setup.art: A big chalk figure of eight on a courtyard floor, a heart drawn where the loops cross, LUNGS written at the top loop and a basket at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big figure of eight with chalk. Mark the heart, lungs and body.

setup.art: A pile of scrunched-up paper balls beside the word LUNGS.
setup.caption: 2. Put paper oxygen balls at the lungs and a basket at the body.

setup.art: Children running round the loop carrying paper balls, one dropping two balls into the body basket.
setup.caption: 3. Run round, carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body.

flow.do: 1. Draw the figure of eight with chalk, big enough to run round. 2. Mark the heart, lungs and body basket. 3. Make 30 paper balls.
flow.say: Today you are red blood cells. This chalk shape is the path your blood takes. Top loop, the lungs. Bottom loop, the body. Every trip goes through the heart in the middle.
flow.kid: You are a red blood cell! The top loop goes to the lungs. The bottom loop goes to the body. Always go through the heart in the middle.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Chalk Heart Relay, a running game about blood carrying oxygen. Here you draw the path.

flow.do: 1. Draw a caller card. 2. Everyone moves at that speed for one minute. 3. Count the balls in the basket and write it down. 4. Empty the basket back at the lungs. 5. Do 4 or 5 cards.
flow.say: Card says: sleeping. Tiptoe round, slowly. Count! Next card: running a race! Go!
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Move at that speed. Carry 2 oxygen balls each trip. After one minute, count the balls in the basket.

check.q: In the Chalk Heart Relay, more oxygen reached the body basket during the 'running a race' minute than the 'sleeping' minute. Why?
options: The red blood cells went round faster, like blood does when the heart beats faster
There were more players
The basket got bigger
check.why: When you run, the heart beats faster, so blood goes round more quickly. Faster trips deliver more oxygen to the muscles that need it. Picking 'more players' is a sensible thing to check, but the players stayed the same. Only the speed changed.

flow.do: Compare the score sheet numbers. Then feel your own pulses.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. Running delivered the most. Now feel your own pulse after all that running. Your real heart did the same thing as our game.
flow.kid: Look at the numbers. Which minute delivered the most oxygen? Now feel your real pulse. Is it fast?
flow.think: Your heart speeds up even when you feel scared, sitting still. Why might your body get ready to run before you even move?

projects.title: Our Family Heart Map

materials.item: a clock or phone that shows seconds
a big sheet of chart paper and colour pencils
the funnel stethoscope from the stethoscope activity, if you made it

projects.safety: Only count pulses of people who say yes. Grandparents and anyone with a heart condition should not do the stair part. Feel a pet's heartbeat only if the pet is calm and its owner says yes.

schedule.what: Count the resting pulse and breaths per minute of everyone at home who agrees. Write their ages.
Count pulses again after climbing one floor of stairs or walking fast for 2 minutes, for those who can. Count a sleeping person's breaths.
Make a big bar chart poster of everyone's resting pulse. Look for a pattern with age. Share it at dinner.

projects.record: Make a table of each person's name, age, resting pulse, pulse after stairs, and breaths per minute. Then draw a bar chart poster.
projects.context: In this 3-day project, you measure the heartbeats and breathing of everyone in your home. Then you make a poster that shows whose heart beats fastest and look for a pattern.

setup.art: A child gently holding a grandmother's wrist, counting, with a notebook open beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Count each person's pulse for 30 seconds, sitting still. Double it.

setup.art: A child watching a sleeping younger brother's chest rise and fall, counting on fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Count breaths in one minute by watching a chest rise and fall.

setup.art: A big chart-paper poster with coloured bars for each family member, labelled with names and ages.

flow.do: 1. Make a table with columns: name, age, resting pulse, pulse after stairs, breaths per minute. 2. For each person who agrees, let them sit for 2 minutes. 3. Your child counts their pulse for 30 seconds and doubles it. 4. Then count their breaths for one minute by watching their chest, without telling them, because people breathe differently when they know they are watched.
flow.say: You're going to be the family's heart doctor. Ask each person politely if you may count their pulse. Then sit them down for two minutes first.

flow.parent: Typical resting pulses: a baby may be 100 to 160, a child 70 to 110, a grown-up 60 to 100. Very fit people can be lower. A breath is one rise and one fall of the chest.

flow.do: 1. Those who can, climb one floor of stairs or walk fast for 2 minutes. 2. Count their pulse straight after. 3. At bedtime, quietly count a sleeping person's breaths for one minute.

check.q: Your little brother breathes 24 times a minute asleep. Your father breathes 14 times. What is the most likely reason?
options: Younger, smaller people usually breathe faster
Your brother is ill
Your father is holding his breath
check.why: Smaller bodies usually breathe faster and have faster hearts, like the mouse and the elephant. A child breathing 24 times a minute asleep is normal. Picking 'ill' is a worry many people have, but a faster rate in a child is usual.

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart poster with one bar for each person's resting pulse. 2. Put the people in order of age. 3. Look for a pattern. 4. Share the poster at dinner and ask everyone what they notice.
flow.say: Let's put everyone in order of age and draw their bars. Do you see a pattern?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each person. Put them in order from youngest to oldest. Is there a pattern? Show your family at dinner.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day.

good: The youngest have the fastest hearts.
People who exercise a lot have slower resting hearts.

flow.think: If every heart in your family beats about 100,000 times a day, how many beats is that for your whole family each day?

challenges.title: Build a One-Way Pump
challenges.problem: Your heart is a pump with flap doors, so blood only goes one way. Your job is to move one cup of water from one bowl to another, using a pump you build, without tipping or pouring the bowls.
constraints: You may not tip, lift or pour either bowl.
You may only use things you find at home.
The water must travel through a tube or bottle you squeeze, like a heart.
materials: two bowls, one full of water and one empty
an empty squeezy bottle, like a shampoo or sauce bottle
a balloon, a turkey baster or a dropper, if you have them
general: Squeeze the bottle, put its mouth under the water, and let go. Water is pushed in. Then lift it over the empty bowl and squeeze. That is how a heart fills and empties.
Use a dropper or a turkey baster, which work the same way, for small amounts.
Count how many squeezes it takes to move one cup. Your heart moves about a cup of blood in a few beats.
creative: Make a flap door from a piece of balloon taped over the end of a straw, so water can go out but not back in. That is a valve, like in your heart.
Make a siphon: fill a tube with water, hold one end in the full bowl and let the other end hang lower into the empty bowl. Water flows by itself.
Squeeze a water balloon with a small hole in rhythm, about once a second, and see how far your 'heart' can push water.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own pump. Draw it, build it and test it. How many squeezes does it need to move one cup? Can you beat your first try?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a pump, like a heart, to move water from one bowl to another without pouring.

flow.do: Read out the problem and the rules. Ask your child to guess how many squeezes it will take.
flow.say: Your heart squeezes blood along without ever pouring. Can you move this cup of water the same way? No tipping the bowls!
flow.kid: Move the water from the full bowl to the empty one. No tipping, no pouring. Only squeezing. Guess how many squeezes it will take.
flow.context: This is the first step of the one-way pump challenge. You build a squeezing pump, like a heart, to move water.

flow.do: Let your child try their own idea first, with the squeezy bottle. Count the squeezes.
flow.say: Try it your way first. I'll count the squeezes.
flow.kid: Try your own way first. Count your squeezes.

check.q: When you let go of a squeezed bottle under water, water rushes in. Why?
options: The bottle springs back to its shape and makes room, so the water outside pushes in
The bottle sucks with a muscle
Water likes plastic
check.why: When the squeezed bottle springs back, there is more room inside. The water outside is pushed in to fill it. Your heart fills the same way when it relaxes. Your lungs fill the same way when the diaphragm makes room. Picking 'sucks with a muscle' is how it feels, but the bottle has no muscle. It just makes room.

flow.do: Now try adding a flap door, a valve, to the straw.
flow.say: Real hearts have flap doors called valves. Let's make one and see if it helps the water go only one way.
flow.kid: Make a little flap door from balloon and tape. Put it on the end of the straw. Does the water go only one way now?
flow.think: What would happen in your heart if a valve did not close properly?

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here is what most people do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways, and some creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: The first artificial hearts were built by engineers and doctors working together. What would you need to make a pump that works for 80 years?

challenges.title: The Best Home Stethoscope
challenges.problem: Design the stethoscope that lets you hear a heartbeat most clearly, using only things from home.
constraints: Nothing may go inside the ear. The tube end rests at the opening only.
Test every design on the same person, sitting still, in the same quiet room.
materials: plastic tube or a hose piece
general: A rolled-up paper tube, like the very first stethoscope made by René Laennec in 1816.
A funnel joined to a plastic tube.
A paper cup with a hole in the bottom, held with its open side on the chest.
creative: Use two tubes joined with a Y-shaped piece, so both ears can listen at once, like a real doctor's stethoscope.
Stretch a piece of balloon over the wide end of a funnel, like the flat disc on a real stethoscope.
Try a long garden hose. Does a longer tube make the sound louder or softer?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Draw it, build it and score how clear the heartbeat sounds from 1 to 5. Which design wins?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build several home-made stethoscopes, the doctor's listening tool, and test which lets you hear a heartbeat best.

flow.do: Build three designs together: a paper tube, a funnel with a tube and a paper cup with a hole.
flow.say: Let's build three listening tools. Then we'll test which is best.
flow.kid: Build three listening tools. Make a paper tube. Make a funnel with a tube. Make a cup with a hole.
flow.context: This is the first step of the best home stethoscope challenge. You build three listening tools to compare.

flow.do: Test each design on the same person, in the same quiet place on the chest. Score each one from 1, can hardly hear, to 5, very clear.
flow.say: To be fair, we test them all on the same person, in the same spot. Give each one a score from 1 to 5.
flow.kid: Test each tool on the same person, same spot. Score it 1 to 5. 5 means very clear.

check.q: Why should you test all the designs on the same person, in the same spot?
options: So only the design changes, and the test is fair
Because other people don't have hearts
To save time
check.why: If you changed the person or the spot, you would not know whether the design or the person made the difference. Changing only one thing makes it a fair test. Picking 'to save time' is a nice bonus, but it is not the reason.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas, then build a new design and test it.
flow.say: Here are some other ideas. Can you invent a better one and beat your best score?
