flow.think: Helen Taussig felt heartbeats with her fingers instead of her ears. Could you design a tool for someone who cannot hear?

items.p: What does the heart do?
opts: It pumps blood round the body
items.why: The heart is a muscle pump. It squeezes to push blood all round the body. Picking 'makes us think' is an old idea people had for thousands of years, but thinking happens in the brain.
items.art: A heart with arrows of blood going out to a body outline.

items.p: About how big is your heart?
opts: As big as your whole chest
items.why: Your heart is about the size of your own fist. It grows as you grow. Picking 'whole chest' usually comes from feeling it beat all over the chest. The lungs fill most of the chest.

items.p: Blood goes away from the heart in tubes called ____, and comes back in tubes called ____.
items.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry it back. A way to remember: Artery and Away both start with A.

items.p: We breathe in a gas called ____ and breathe out a gas called ____.
items.why: We take in oxygen, which every cell needs. We breathe out carbon dioxide, the waste gas cells make.

items.p: Your lungs have muscles that suck air in.
items.why: False. Lungs have no muscles of their own. The diaphragm under them pulls down and makes room, and the air outside pushes in.

items.p: The blood in your veins is blue.
items.why: False. Blood is always red. Blood with less oxygen is darker red. Veins only look blue through skin.

items.p: Your heart beats even when you are asleep.
items.why: True. Your heart beats all the time, day and night. It slows down a little when you sleep.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
items.why: Each part has one main job in moving blood and air.
pairs: pulls down to help you breathe in

items.p: Where is the best place to feel your pulse?
opts: The thumb side of the inside of your wrist
items.why: An artery runs close to the skin on the thumb side of the wrist, so you can feel it bulge with each heartbeat. Picking the elbow bone or the head usually means looking for the beat where something is hard. You need a soft place where an artery is near the skin.

items.p: Why should you feel your pulse with your fingers, not your thumb?
opts: Your thumb has its own pulse, which can confuse you
items.why: Your thumb has an artery in it with its own pulse. You might count your own thumb's beat instead of the wrist's. Fingers have a weaker pulse at the tip, so they work better.

items.p: Sort these. Do they make your heart beat FASTER or SLOWER?
items.why: Moving hard and feeling scared or excited speed the heart up. Rest, sleep and slow breathing slow it down.
items: being scared by a loud bang
slow breathing in for 4, out for 6

items.p: In the jumping heart experiment, you counted 40 beats in 30 seconds while sitting still. How many is that in one minute?
items.why: One minute is two lots of 30 seconds, so double 40. 40 + 40 = 80. Picking 20 usually means halving instead of doubling.
items.context: This question is about the jumping heart experiment. You count your pulse at your wrist while sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after resting.

items.p: Why do you breathe faster when you run? Use the word oxygen in your answer.
items.a: When I run, my muscles work hard and need more oxygen to get energy from food. So I breathe faster to get more oxygen in, and my heart beats faster to carry it to my muscles.
items.why: Running muscles need extra oxygen, and they make extra carbon dioxide. Faster breathing brings oxygen in and takes carbon dioxide out.

items.p: Draw a heart in the middle of a body outline. Draw red arrows to show blood going out to the head, the arms and the legs, and coming back.
items.a: Arrows go out from the heart to the head, arms and legs, and other arrows come back to the heart, making loops.
items.why: Blood always goes out from the heart and comes back to it. That is why it is called circulation, from the word circle.
items.art: A blank body outline with a heart shape in the chest.

items.p: Label the picture: windpipe, lungs, diaphragm, heart.
items.a: The windpipe is the tube at the top. The two lungs are on each side. The heart is between them, in the middle. The diaphragm is the dome muscle underneath.
items.why: The heart sits between the lungs. The diaphragm is under them both. The windpipe carries air down to the lungs.
items.art: An outline of a chest with a ringed tube, two lungs, a heart between them and a dome muscle below, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Which helps keep your lungs healthy?
opts: Playing outside and staying away from smoke
items.why: Exercise makes your lungs and breathing muscles strong, and smoke and dust harm the lungs. Picking 'never running' usually means thinking getting out of breath is bad. Getting out of breath while playing is good for you.

worksheets.title: Two Circles and a Great Swap (stretch)

items.p: A drop of blood leaves the right side of your heart. Where does it go first?
items.why: The right side of the heart sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. It comes back to the left side, which sends it to the body. Picking 'brain' or 'toes' usually means picturing just one loop.

items.p: Why is the wall of the left side of the heart thicker than the right?
opts: It must push blood all round the body, not just to the lungs next door
items.why: The left side pushes blood the long way, all over the body. The right side only pushes it a short way, to the lungs. A bigger job needs a stronger muscle.

items.p: Which air has more carbon dioxide?
items.why: Your cells make carbon dioxide when they use food for energy. Your blood carries it to the lungs and you breathe it out. Breathed-out air has about 100 times more carbon dioxide than room air.

items.p: In the milky breath experiment, why did the limewater turn milky?
opts: Carbon dioxide from the breath reacted with the lime
items.why: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide passes through it. Breath has lots of carbon dioxide. Picking 'oxygen' is a common mix-up. Room air has more oxygen than breath, but the room-air glass stayed clear.
items.context: This question is about the milky breath experiment. Limewater is made by stirring chuna into water and letting it settle. You blew your breath through one glass and pushed room air through another.

items.p: Put the path of air in order, from outside to the blood.
items.why: Air goes in through the nose, down the windpipe, along branching tubes, into the tiny air sacs, and then oxygen passes into the blood.

items.p: The air you breathe out has no oxygen left in it.
items.why: False. Breathed-out air still has about 16 parts oxygen in every 100. You only use a little with each breath. That is why a rescue breath can help someone.

items.p: Your heart makes its own beat, even without a message from the brain each time.
items.why: True. A small patch of pacemaker cells in the heart makes a tiny electric spark again and again. The brain only speeds it up or slows it down.

items.p: Why are the walls of the air sacs so thin?
opts: So oxygen can pass through them into the blood quickly
items.why: The wall between the air and the blood is thinner than a soap bubble. Thin walls let oxygen and carbon dioxide slip across fast. Picking 'so they can pop' comes from thinking of bubbles, but healthy air sacs do not pop.

items.p: Every cell uses ____ to break up food and get energy out. This is called respiration.
items.why: Cells join oxygen with food to release energy. Carbon dioxide and water are left over.

items.p: A pulse watcher is a toothpick stuck in a dough ball on your wrist. Why does it tick?
opts: The artery under it bulges each time the heart pushes blood
items.why: Each heartbeat sends a push of blood that makes the artery bulge a tiny bit. The bulge tips the toothpick. Picking 'bones move' is a fair guess, but your arm is still. The ticks match your heartbeat.
items.context: A pulse watcher is a toothpick standing in a pea-sized ball of dough, placed over the pulse on your wrist.

items.p: In the bottle lung model, the stretched balloon at the bottom stands for which part of you?
items.why: The stretchy bottom is the diaphragm, the dome muscle under your lungs. Pulling it down makes room, and the lung balloon fills. The bottle's neck is the windpipe.
items.context: The bottle lung is a model of breathing made from a cut-off plastic bottle, a balloon inside it as a lung, and another balloon stretched across the bottom.

items.p: Match the person to what they did.
items.why: Each of these people helped us understand the heart and blood.
pairs: said blood goes from the heart to the lungs and back
showed blood goes round and round
felt heartbeats with her fingers and helped save blue babies

items.p: In the story, why did the blue babies turn pink after the operation?
items.a: The new pipe sent more blood to the lungs. In the lungs the blood picked up oxygen and turned bright red. So the babies' lips turned pink.
items.why: Blood only picks up oxygen when it goes through the lungs. More blood to the lungs means more oxygen in the body.

items.p: Your heart and breathing both speed up when you exercise. Why do they work as a team?
items.a: The lungs bring oxygen into the blood, and the heart pushes that blood to the muscles. If only one sped up, the muscles would not get enough oxygen.
items.why: Breathing gets oxygen into the blood. The heart moves the blood. The muscles need both.

items.p: Lobsters and octopuses have blue blood. Why?
opts: They carry oxygen with copper instead of iron
items.why: Our red cells carry oxygen with iron, which looks red. Lobster and octopus blood carries oxygen with copper, which looks blue. Picking 'blue water' usually means thinking colour comes from the place an animal lives.

items.p: Draw the figure of eight of blood. Put the heart in the middle, the lungs on the top loop, and the body on the bottom loop. Colour blood bright red after the lungs and darker red after the body.
items.a: A figure-of-eight with the heart in the middle, bright red going from the lungs to the heart and out to the body, darker red coming back from the body to the heart and on to the lungs.
items.why: Blood gets bright red in the lungs, where it picks up oxygen. It gets darker red in the body, where it gives oxygen away.
items.art: A blank figure of eight with a small heart where the loops cross.

items.p: William Harvey worked out that a heart pumps out more blood in an hour than the weight of a whole person. What did this prove?
opts: The same blood must go round again and again
The liver makes lots of blood
People drink a lot of water
items.why: No body could make or eat that much blood every hour. So it must be the same blood, coming back to the heart over and over. Picking 'the liver makes lots' was Galen's old idea, which Harvey's sum showed could not be true.

items.p: Ibn al-Nafis described blood going through the lungs around 1242. Why did European doctors not learn about it for hundreds of years?
opts: His book was in Arabic and was forgotten, then found again in 1924
items.why: His work was right, but it was written in Arabic and not widely read in Europe. It was found again in a library in 1924. Picking 'he was wrong' is not true. He was right, centuries early. Who is remembered depends on who could read your work.

items.p: A mouse's heart beats about 500 times a minute. An elephant's beats about 30 times. Which is the most likely reason?
opts: Small animals lose heat fast, so their cells burn food fast and need oxygen fast
items.why: Small bodies have lots of skin for their size and lose heat quickly. To stay warm, their cells must work fast, and that needs oxygen fast. So the heart beats fast. Picking 'mice are always scared' is a fun guess, but even calm mice have fast hearts.

items.p: When you hold your breath, the strong urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up in your blood.
items.why: True. Your brain watches the carbon dioxide in your blood. When it builds up, the brain makes you want to breathe very strongly. Running low on oxygen matters less to this feeling.

items.p: Plants only make oxygen and never use it.
items.why: False. Plants respire day and night, using oxygen like us. In sunlight they also make much more oxygen than they use.

items.p: Some of the oxygen atoms in your body were made inside stars, long before the Earth existed. What does this mean?
opts: The stuff you breathe and are made of has come a very long way
You are hot like a star
Oxygen is made only in your lungs
items.why: Oxygen atoms were made inside stars and scattered when those stars died. Later they became part of Earth's air and water, and now part of you. Picking 'made only in your lungs' mixes up making oxygen with using it. Lungs only take it in.

items.p: A person gets a new heart from a donor. The nerves from the brain are not joined to the new heart. What happens?
opts: The new heart still beats, by its own pacemaker spark
The person needs to think 'beat' every second
The brain grows a new nerve that same day
items.why: The heart makes its own beat with its pacemaker cells. Nerves only speed it up or slow it down. Picking 'needs to think beat' usually means thinking the brain controls every heartbeat.

items.p: Breathing runs by itself, but you can also control it. Why might it be useful that you can control your breathing?
items.a: So I can hold my breath under water, blow out candles, speak and sing, and calm myself down by breathing slowly.
items.why: Speaking, singing, swimming and calming down all need control over breath. Your brain lets you take over for a while, then takes back control.

items.p: Is your breath part of you, or part of the world? Explain your thinking.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: It is both. The air was outside me, then inside me, and then goes back out to plants and other people.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer notices that the same air moves in and out, so the line between me and the world is not sharp.

items.p: At the top of a high mountain, people breathe faster. Why?
opts: Each breath has less oxygen in it, so they need more breaths
items.why: High up, the air is thinner. Each breath brings in less oxygen, so you breathe faster to get enough. People who live high up, in Ladakh for example, grow used to this over time. Picking 'colder' is true about mountains, but it is not the main reason for fast breathing.

items.p: Helen Taussig could hardly hear. How did she study hearts?
opts: She felt the heartbeats with her fingers
She used a very loud speaker
items.why: She learned to feel the push and rush of blood through her fingertips on the chest. There is more than one way to listen. Picking 'did not study hearts' is not true. She became one of the most important children's heart doctors of her time.

items.p: Sort these. Is it true now, or an old idea that was shown wrong?
items.why: Old ideas were changed when people looked, measured and counted more carefully.
items: Blood soaks through holes in the heart's middle wall
The heart is where we think
The heart makes its own beat
Blood is made fresh and used up like fuel
Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs

items.p: Grown-up heart muscle can hardly repair itself, but a zebrafish can grow back part of its heart. Why do you think scientists study zebrafish hearts?
items.a: To find out how the fish repairs its heart, so one day doctors might help human hearts repair themselves after damage.
items.why: Learning how other animals do something can give us ideas for helping people. This is still being studied.

items.p: Why do you think the lungs are folded into hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, instead of being two big empty bags?
opts: Many tiny sacs have a huge surface, so lots of oxygen can pass into the blood at once
items.why: Many tiny bubbles have far more surface than one big bag. More surface means more places for oxygen to cross into the blood. Spread flat, a grown-up's air sacs would cover nearly a badminton court.

items.p: Your red blood cells only live about four months. New ones replace them all the time. Are you the same person you were a year ago? Explain.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: My blood is new, but I still remember things and I am still me. So maybe I am more like a river than a stone.
items.why: There is no single right answer. This is a question people have argued about for thousands of years.

items.p: Why can't we breathe on the Moon, even with strong lungs?
opts: There is no air there to push into our lungs
items.why: Breathing in works because air outside pushes in when the diaphragm makes room. On the Moon there is no air at all, so nothing can push in. Astronauts take their own air with them.

quiz.why: The heart is a hollow muscle that squeezes to push blood round the body. Picking 'a bag of air' mixes it up with the lungs.

quiz.p: Where does blood go after it leaves the heart?
opts: Round the body and back to the heart
Into the stomach to be used up
quiz.why: Blood goes round in a loop and always comes back to the heart. Picking 'used up' was Galen's old idea, which William Harvey showed was wrong.

quiz.p: You counted 48 heartbeats in 30 seconds. How many is that in a minute?
quiz.why: One minute is two lots of 30 seconds, so double it. 48 + 48 = 96. Picking 24 means halving instead of doubling.
quiz.context: This question is about the jumping heart experiment. You count your pulse at your wrist while sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after resting.

quiz.p: In the jumping heart experiment, when was the pulse fastest?
quiz.why: Just after jumping, the muscles needed the most oxygen, so the heart beat fastest. Picking 'after rest' usually means thinking the heart keeps speeding up after you stop. It starts slowing straight away.
quiz.context: This question is about the jumping heart experiment. You count your pulse at your wrist while sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after resting.

quiz.p: Why do we count the pulse two times?
opts: Because one count can be a mistake
To make the heart beat faster
quiz.why: Anyone can lose count once. Two counts that agree make us more sure. Picking 'two wrists' is a funny guess, but we count on the same wrist both times.

quiz.p: What happens when your diaphragm pulls down?
opts: Your chest gets bigger and air flows into your lungs
quiz.why: The diaphragm pulling down makes room in your chest, and air pushes in to fill it. Picking 'air is pushed out' is the opposite: that happens when it relaxes and goes up.

quiz.p: Which gas do your cells need, and which do they make as waste?
quiz.why: Cells need oxygen to get energy from food, and make carbon dioxide as waste. Plants do the swap the other way in sunlight. Picking 'need carbon dioxide' mixes us up with plants.

quiz.p: What do red blood cells carry?
quiz.why: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to every part of the body. Picking 'germs' mixes them up with white blood cells, which fight germs.

quiz.p: Which part of blood helps plug a cut?
quiz.why: Platelets are tiny pieces that stick together to plug a cut and help make a scab. Plasma is the watery yellow part that carries food.

quiz.p: You feel scared, and your heart starts pounding even though you are sitting still. Why?
opts: Your body is getting ready to run, just in case
quiz.why: Fear gets the body ready for action. The heart speeds up to send more oxygen to the muscles. Picking 'heart is broken' comes from words like 'heartbroken', but a pounding heart is healthy.

quiz.p: Which is the best way to calm a fast heart?
opts: Slow breathing, with a long breath out
Holding your breath as long as you can
quiz.why: A long slow breath out sends a calming message to the heart. Picking 'holding your breath' is not a good idea. It can make you feel worse.

quiz.p: Which is good for your heart and lungs?
quiz.why: Exercise makes the heart and lungs strong. Smoke harms them. Getting out of breath while playing is good for you.

quiz.p: Who showed in 1628 that blood goes round and round the body?
quiz.why: William Harvey counted, measured and tested, and showed blood circulates. Galen believed blood was made and used up. Laennec invented the stethoscope much later, in 1816.

quiz.p: Ibn al-Nafis, a doctor in Cairo about 780 years ago, said something new. What was it?
opts: Blood goes from the heart to the lungs and back
The heart is where we think
quiz.why: He said blood goes from the right side of the heart, through the lungs, to the left side. He was right, but his book was forgotten in Europe for centuries.

quiz.p: Why do your cells need oxygen?
opts: To get energy out of food
quiz.why: Every cell joins oxygen with food to release energy. This is called respiration. Picking 'don't need it' is not true: without oxygen, most of our cells would stop working in minutes.

quiz.p: Where does most of the oxygen in the air come from?
opts: Plants on land and tiny algae in the sea
quiz.why: Plants and tiny algae in the sea give out oxygen when they make food in sunlight. Scientists estimate about half comes from the sea. Our lungs only take oxygen in.

maths.problem: In the jumping heart experiment, Meera counted 42 heartbeats in 30 seconds while sitting still. How many heartbeats is that in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 60 seconds. That is two lots of 30 seconds. So Meera's heart beat 42 times, and then 42 times again. 42 + 42 = 84. Another way: 40 + 40 = 80, and 2 + 2 = 4, so 84.
maths.context: This question is about the jumping heart experiment. You count your pulse at your wrist while sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after resting.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a whole minute is hard, and children lose count. Counting for half a minute and doubling gives the same answer with fewer mistakes.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart from the jumping heart experiment. Sitting still, the heart beat 88 times a minute. Just after jumping, it beat 148 times a minute. How many more beats a minute was that?
maths.explain: We take the smaller number away from the bigger one. 148 take away 88. First take away 80: 148 - 80 = 68. Then take away 8 more: 68 - 8 = 60. So jumping added 60 beats a minute. Check: 88 + 60 = 148.
maths.context: This question is about the jumping heart experiment. You count your pulse at your wrist while sitting still, just after one minute of jumping, and after resting.

chart.title: Made-up example results: heartbeats in one minute
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which bar is tallest. Taking one bar from another tells us exactly how much the heart sped up.

maths.problem: In the upside-down bottle experiment, Kabir's ordinary breath out pushed out 250 ml of air. His biggest breath out pushed out 1,500 ml. How many ordinary breaths would fit into his biggest breath?
maths.explain: We want to know how many lots of 250 make 1,500. Count up: 250, 500, 750, 1,000, 1,250, 1,500. That is 6 jumps. So his biggest breath was 6 times his ordinary one.
maths.context: This is about the upside-down bottle experiment. A bottle full of water stands upside down in a bucket. When you breathe out through a tube into it, the air pushes water out, and the marks show how much air you breathed out.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'my big breath is bigger' is a start. Saying 'it is 6 times bigger' tells us exactly how much spare room our lungs keep for running and singing.

maths.problem: A child's heart pushes out about 40 ml of blood with each beat. That is about 8 teaspoons. A child has about 2,000 ml of blood in all. How many heartbeats does it take to push out 2,000 ml?
maths.answer: 50 heartbeats, which is less than one minute.
maths.explain: 10 beats push out 10 lots of 40 ml. That is 400 ml. 2,000 ml is 5 lots of 400 ml. So it takes 5 lots of 10 beats. That is 50 beats. A child's heart beats about 90 times a minute, so 50 beats takes well under a minute. This is the kind of sum William Harvey did. The heart pushes out all your blood in less than a minute. So the same blood must go round and round.
maths.context: This is about the jumping heart experiment, where you counted how many times your heart beats in a minute. Now we use the beats to work out how fast all your blood goes round. The amounts are rough, for a child of about 8.
maths.why_maths: In 1628 William Harvey used a sum like this to prove that blood goes round in a circle. Simple multiplying changed medicine.

maths.problem: In the squeeze like a heart activity, you squeezed a ball about 100 times in one minute, like a fast child's heart. How many squeezes would that be in one hour?
maths.explain: There are 60 minutes in an hour. Each minute has 100 squeezes. 60 lots of 100 is 6,000. Your heart does about this many beats every hour, all day and all night. In one day it is about 100,000 beats.
maths.context: This is about the squeeze like a heart activity. You squeeze a ball once every time your heart beats, to feel how hard the heart works.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers are hard to feel. Building them up from one minute you have felt helps you understand how hard your heart really works.

applications: Doctors use stethoscopes to listen to the heart and lungs at every check-up.
A small clip on the fingertip, called a pulse oximeter, measures the pulse and how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Many families bought one during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Ambulances and hospitals give oxygen from cylinders to people who cannot get enough by breathing.
A doctor's ECG machine reads the heart's own electric sparks and draws them as a wavy line.
Blood donation: one healthy grown-up's donated blood can help save the life of someone after an accident or an operation.
Pacemakers are tiny battery-powered devices that make the heart's spark for people whose own pacemaker cells do not work well.
The 'blue baby' operation from the story, and later heart surgery, has helped many thousands of children grow up.
Rescue breathing and chest pressing, called CPR, can keep blood and oxygen moving when someone's heart has stopped, until help comes.
Divers, firefighters and astronauts carry tanks of air, because they go where there is no good air to breathe.
Air quality boards in Indian cities show how dirty the air is, so people with weak lungs can stay indoors on bad days.
Athletes count their resting pulse. A lower resting pulse often means a fitter heart.
Singers, shehnai players and people who blow the shankh train their breathing to hold long notes.
Yoga breathing, called pranayama, is taught in schools and parks across India to help people feel calm.

open_questions.q: Why can a grown-up human heart hardly repair itself, when a zebrafish can grow back part of its heart?
open_questions.why_open: In 2009, scientists used a trace left in people's bodies by old bomb tests to measure how fast heart muscle cells are replaced. In young adults, only about 1 in every 100 is replaced each year. Zebrafish can regrow a damaged part in weeks. Nobody yet knows how to make human hearts do this.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the very first heartbeat start in a tiny growing baby?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can watch the first beats in tiny embryos of animals. How the cells first learn to beat together, all at once, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How much do signals from the heart shape what we feel and think?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show heart signals can change how scary something seems. How big this effect is, and how it works, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How do naked mole-rats survive about 18 minutes with no oxygen at all?
open_questions.why_open: In 2017, scientists found these underground rodents can switch to burning a different sugar when oxygen runs out. How they protect their brains and hearts is still being studied. It might one day help people after a heart attack or stroke.

open_questions.q: Is there really a 'budget' of heartbeats in a lifetime?
open_questions.why_open: Many mammals have about a billion heartbeats in a life, but there are many exceptions, and nobody knows if the pattern means anything deep.

open_questions.q: How long are all your blood vessels, laid end to end?
open_questions.why_open: A number often quoted is about 100,000 kilometres for a grown-up, but it is a rough guess. The tiniest vessels are very hard to count, and some scientists think the real number could be quite different.

open_questions.q: Could people one day get a new heart or lung grown in a laboratory from their own cells?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have grown tiny beating heart balls and small lung pieces from cells. Growing a whole working organ is still far away, and nobody knows when or if it will be possible.

open_questions.q: Why do some peoples who have lived high in the mountains for thousands of years cope so well with thin air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found some genes that help Tibetan people live with less oxygen. How all the pieces work together, in Ladakh, the Andes and elsewhere, is still being studied.

roots.context: We have been learning how the heart pumps blood round and round, and how the lungs swap air with the world. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You are not a still thing. You are a flow that the world keeps passing through.
deep_truth.habit: We think of 'me' as a fixed thing with a clear edge, and the air and other people as outside. But air comes into you, becomes part of your blood and cells, and goes out again to trees and other people. Even your blood is replaced every few months. The edge between you and the world is a doorway, not a wall.
deep_truth.evidence: Every breath swaps air with the room. Every minute, all your blood goes round once. Your red blood cells are all new in about four months. And the carbon dioxide you breathe out becomes part of a plant.

three.who_am_i: You are a heart that never stops and a breath that is always moving. The air you are made of was the world's a moment ago.
three.what_is_life: Living things keep taking in and giving out. A heartbeat and a breath are life saying 'still going'.
three.what_is_this_world: It is a world where trees breathe out what you breathe in, and you breathe out what trees breathe in.

roots.thread: Before you breathe in, the air belongs to the whole world. Inside you, it becomes your blood, your warmth and your thinking. When you breathe out, it belongs to the world again. The same oxygen, made long ago in stars, has passed through trees, tigers, grandmothers and you. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many bodies, all sharing one breath. Your heart and lungs are where the many meet the one shared air.

teachings.teaching: The senses argued about which of them was the greatest. Speech left the body for a year, and the body lived on, unable to speak. The eye left, and the ear left, and the mind left, and still the body lived. Then breath began to leave, and all the others were pulled along with it, like pegs torn up by a horse. They agreed that breath was the greatest of them all.
teachings.link: Science agrees that breath and heartbeat keep every other part going. Without oxygen carried by blood, the eyes, ears and brain soon stop working.

teachings.source: Kabir, Songs of Kabir, poem I, translated by Rabindranath Tagore (1915)
teachings.teaching: Kabir says the one people search for in temples and mosques is right beside them. He ends: God is the breath of all breath.
teachings.link: The breath we share with every living thing is the closest thing to us. Kabir pointed there, not far away.

teachings.teaching: A Vietnamese Buddhist teacher taught a simple practice. Breathing in, I calm my body. Breathing out, I smile. Paying gentle attention to the breath brings us back to the present moment.
teachings.link: Slow breathing really does calm the heart, as you can feel with your own pulse.

science.text: Most oxygen atoms in the air and in you were made inside stars long ago. Plants and algae put oxygen into the air, and the carbon dioxide you breathe out is taken in by plants.

Air mixes all round the Earth over the years. Some scientists have worked out that each breath you take probably holds a few of the same molecules that any one person breathed out long ago. This is a rough calculation, not a measurement.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Breath is air moving in and out of a body, and blood is a liquid pumped by a muscle. That fully explains it. There is no need for any One behind it. When the body stops, the breath and the person stop too. This is an honest view held by many thoughtful people.
